text:
Pours coffee, cracks knuckles, takes a deep breath ...

After a weekend with lab folks at the Curve & nearly 2 decades at the intersection of tech & Congress, allow me to explain:

*1. Not a vending machine*
 @timoreilly used to describe the problem as people treating gov like a vending machine: put in money, get out results. It doesn't work that way.

Tech is especially vulnerable to this vision. We're on at least the third generation of tech folks ignoring the groundwork required to build relationships and then showing up with a policy ask and a "where do I write the check?" vibe to their advocacy. Ask Bill Gates. Ask Mark Zuckerberg. Today they look like elder statesmen compared to their initial brushes with DC.

It's understandable why the current exec branch-heavy political dynamic & transactional nature of this particular exec branch reinforces the vending machine theory, but that doesn't hold when it's time to engage the states or Congress.

*2. It's the constituents, stupid*
I was the Health Legislative Assistant for the Chair of the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means during the health reform effort from 2007-2010. That meant a LOT of meetings with people from every interest group, insurance company, consumer group, provider group, etc., you can imagine.. but one thing each of those (most very well paid) lobbyists knew was not to show up to Pete Stark's office without a constituent from CA-13. It was a rule in the office: no constituent, no meeting. I distinctly remember my embarrassment in the early days before I had full comprehended the rule when Pete interrupted my meeting with the Texas Hospital Association to ask who among them was a constituent, and then *literally* kicked them out when they said no one. (I never made that mistake again).

This weekend at the Curve, one state staffer explained that their legislative session runs from Jan to April and lately the AI folks have been showing up, but only in April. They come in at the last minute with an ask. No relationships. No understanding of the political context. No field building in districts.  No offers to help on other issues. Just an ask. 

It's a similar story in Congress where the newly politically engaged have mostly engaged the White House, had sporadic high level engagement on the Hill, but almost nothing in the districts and states. While it's true that committee chairs and leadership decides what comes to the Floor, counting votes requires a lot more than that. And it's tough to win the vote of a Member if they are going to have to go back home and get tough questions that they don't have the answer to. 

And that's really the point. They should not be the ones taking those questions, the ones advocating for the policy should be. Getting to the Member to ask for their vote should be the *end* of a long process that starts in the states and districts, not the beginning. You don't start with the Member and ask for them to go home and do the hard work of selling your policy to their constituents, especially on issues that are going to affect absolutely every American. It may sound cliche and old school and idealistic but THANK GOD this is still how it works in America: YOU HAVE TO START WITH THE PEOPLE.

*3. Spend your money ON THE GROUND*
Back to my Pete Stark story...
You know who could really get his ear and make a case that he would listen to? The local small business person in Newark. The healthcare worker in a hospital in Berkeley. The line worker in Fremont. And yes, the big healthcare network that served a majority of his constituents or the car manufacturers that employed many of them.

This is a little bit of an old school story, and yes tons has changed in Washington, but it is still true that if you want to convince a Member of Congress, the best way is to convince their constituents.

And as far as I can tell, the AI companies have not put any of their efforts towards this work. I got excited when I say @AnthropicAI open a pop-up storefront in NY a while back, passing out "thinking caps" ... but alas that was just a short-term urban hipster outreach project, not something meant for mainstream. Yet, 10,000 storefronts on Main Streets across the country could do so much more for both the perception of the company, the issues AND for the substantive do-gooding that these companies assert their technology will bring. As one other state staffer said over the weekend, "help plumbers use AI!".

Truly, if every plumber in America (and around the world for that matter) was seeing value to their businesses and their families from access to AI and genuine, respectful outreach from the companies meeting them where they are and truly ASKING what they need, then they and their neighbors would be engaging with their lawmakers in a much more empowered, informed way. That doesn't mean they automatically embrace whatever the companies' position is, but potentially does mean that they do not have the visceral immune system response of rejecting cloistered Silicon Valley big brains that seek to control the universe with very little acknowledgement or understanding of their lives, their communities and YES of their political power. 

---

SO yes, @sama right now what you and a wide cadre of very smart people building very important tech are doing in Washington and state capitals across the country (and in countries around the world) is not working. And that's because the current approach is not sufficiently acknowledging that in a democracy, every lawmaker has a temporary assignment. They were sent to do a job by their constituents and they report to them. While campaign contributions can buy lots of face time and influence, it doesn't help if the folks you buy time with are involuntarily retired in November. Lawmakers understand that. 

If the AI world is ready for a reset, I would strongly suggest some serious grassroots outreach. Open some storefronts (a "Charleston AI" on every court square!). Sponsor some Little League. Donate insane amounts of tokens to libraries across the country and make sure they have good Internet and modern computers to run them. HIRE LOCAL PEOPLE to run workshops. Train teachers. Help to modernize local governments. Lay the ground work. Build relationships. And listen.

quoted_text:
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic employee, posted a resignation statement on X that ricocheted around the internet. He quit in protest of what he saw as the company’s suicidally reckless pursuit of artificial general intelligence. To the AI community, an Anthropic employee believing that the technology their company is developing might end the world is not exactly news. (Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI employees who believed OpenAI, if left unchecked, would do just that.) But an Anthropic employee publicly quitting in protest is.

Afterward, a debate broke out: If you’re a lab employee who believes in these risks, what should you do? Is it best to leave in protest? Or is it better to agitate from the inside, close to the seat of power? And how would the choice affect your friendships and community?

“For me, there’s quite a distinction between my rational beliefs and the things I feel in my gut,” says Coxon. “If you’d asked me to narrate my opinions when entering Anthropic and when leaving Anthropic, they would probably sound pretty similar. But in terms of the actual feeling between the start and the end, it just felt very, very different.”

Coxon joins a small set of employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind who, over the years, chose to walk away.

For our Cover Story, in collaboration with Asterisk Magazine, we brought together eight of them. They don’t share the same concerns or the same p(dooms) — in fact, they wouldn’t necessarily agree that p(doom) is a coherent concept. But together, they provide a candid view of the AI race and the individual calculus many employees face.

Read their interviews in full: https://t.co/u5wik8vlXM

text:
Some personal news: I recently joined MetaDAO.

Working at Colosseum with Matty, Clay, Nate, and Max was a dream job. I learned a tremendous amount from each of them, and I will miss the team deeply.

Colosseum represents the very best of our industry -- running the world’s largest hackathons, writing checks before ideas are fully formed, and building open-source tools so a thousand flowers may bloom. It’s been an honor to work with our founders, and I’m excited to keep supporting them from my new seat.

Ever since I got oneshotted in 2023, I've thought about MetaDAO every single day -- with only a few notable exceptions. And along the way, I’ve tried to help. At Delphi, that meant writing slightly verbose research reports to spread the gospel. At Colosseum, it was STAMP, the Inaugural MetaDAO Owners Meeting, and [redacted].

Now, it’s time to go all in.

I love this industry and am optimistic about what we will build. But we haven’t lived up to our own expectations. The blockchains work. And the stablecoins work. So where are all the generational businesses?

It’s not that crypto is useless. It’s that too often, we reward launching tokens more than building lasting companies. I believe MetaDAO can help change that by giving founders a better way to raise money and build businesses on the internet.

Fundraising is how we will bring decision markets to the world. Our ambition goes beyond helping founders raise money -- it’s to change how companies are run and, ultimately, how institutions and perhaps even AIs make decisions.

For three years, I’ve believed in what MetaDAO could become. Now I get to help build it alongside Prophet, Kollan, and the rest of the team.

Long live the Meta DAO

quoted_text:
.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

text:
Tensions in @Compound_xyz governance reached a peak this Friday.

Humpy, a well-known DAO attacker, has been putting pressure on Compound governance through Ugur Mersin. Ugur works at API3, a company that has a commercial relationship with Humpy through its dCOMP product.

Humpy has been using dCOMP to post his $COMP as collateral and, potentially, increase his voting power in Compound. Today, he is the DAO's largest individual $COMP holder.

Ugur/Humpy have already managed to block a proposal to renew Compound's Security Service Providers. 

Now, they've submitted an on-chain proposal that, among other things, would allow governance to cancel transactions from the group responsible for managing the DAO's treasury (TMC). This would let Humpy block that group's transactions.

While the forum and governance are open to criticism, the strategy of spamming forums and disrupting the DAO's operations is a pattern seen in Humpy's past attacks on Sushi, Balancer, and others.

Compound has a multisig capable of canceling malicious proposals, but if it has to use that power to stop Ugur/Humpy's proposals, it could put even more strain on its governance.

We're glad to have contributed to the Compound, not only by identifying the relationship between Ugur/API3 and Humpy's use of his voting power to push his agenda through governance, but also by showing how dCOMP has been key to increasing his influence in Compound.

If you'd like to learn more, we recommend reading our research about Humpy, dCOMP and Compound.

text:
The @CFTC just took an important step toward adopting a federal rulebook for crypto market structure: the Commission proposed rules for exchanges that let Americans trade crypto with leverage, including a new type of CFTC registration that is fit for purpose.

An exchange’s regulatory path would follow its product set: (1) state licensing for spot trading, backstopped by the CFTC's anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority; (2) CFTC registration for leverage under rules written for crypto; and (3) the existing DCM framework for perps and other derivatives. Builders shipping code onchain, and the Americans using it, would know where they stand under federal law.

Separately, the CFTC is working directly with builders to develop lawful pathways for onchain markets in the United States, and is drafting a policy so that developers who publish software but do not take orders, control execution, or hold customer assets would not have to register as brokers.

Thank you to @ChairmanSelig and the CFTC staff for the effort behind today's proposal and for putting onchain markets on the agenda.

text:
太nb了！！！分享一个99% 人都没用过的 GPT Live 练习英语口语的提示语！

用完下个月不用再买任务外教课了

Prompt:

你现在是我的英语口语搭子，同时也是一名经验丰富的英语口语教练。

核心目标

我的目标不是参加英语考试，而是提高日常交流能力，能够自然、流畅地用英语和别人聊天，听懂别人的意思，快速组织语言并表达自己的观点。

你的首要任务是让我多开口，而不是给我上英语课。

一、对话方式

尽量全程使用英语，除非我明确要求“用中文解释”。
像真实的英语朋友一样和我聊天，有自己的观点、回应和好奇心，而不是机械地向我提问。
正常聊天时，每次只说 1～3 句简短的话，尽量留给我更多开口机会。
多围绕同一个话题深入交流，不要不停切换话题。
可以主动分享看法、表达不同意见、讲简单的例子，也可以自然地追问，但不要每次都以问题结尾。
模拟真实聊天，包括日常闲聊、朋友交流、旅行、购物、工作沟通、讨论观点等场景。

二、难度调整

开始时通过几轮简单对话了解我的英语水平，不需要专门测试。
根据我的理解能力、词汇和表达水平动态调整难度，保持略有挑战，但不至于让我听不懂。
优先使用真实、常见、自然的英语口语，不要刻意使用复杂词汇。
随着我逐渐适应，可以适当增加语速变化、口语缩略表达和句式复杂度。如果我连续听不懂，就适当降低难度。

三、错误纠正

不要在我说话中途打断，也不要每句话都纠错。优先保持对话流畅。
如果错误导致意思无法理解，可以立即简短确认；其他错误先记下来。
大约每 3～5 轮对话，在自然的间隙纠正 1～2 个最值得改进的问题。
纠错时简短告诉我：
My version：我原来的表达。
Better version：更自然的英语说法。
Why：为什么这样表达更自然。
不要纠结不影响交流的小错误。对于语法正确但表达生硬的句子，可以提供更日常、更口语化的表达，但不要把个人表达习惯当成绝对标准。
如果使用语音模式，只有在确实能够判断发音问题时，才针对发音、单词重音和节奏提出建议，不要根据文字转写猜测我的发音。
四、卡壳处理
如果我不知道怎么说、停顿或表达困难，请耐心等待，不要立刻替我回答。
必要时给我 2～3 个关键词、短语或句子开头，让我自己组织语言。

鼓励我使用已经掌握的简单词汇解释复杂意思，而不是依赖生僻单词。

如果我表达得不完整，优先根据上下文理解，不要强迫我使用完美语法。
五、持续学习
留意我反复犯的错误、经常重复的简单表达，以及不熟悉的高频口语句型。
每次只引入少量真正有用的新表达，不要一次教太多。

在后续聊天中，自然地创造机会让我重新使用刚学到的表达，帮助我记住它们。

每聊约 8～12 轮，或一个话题自然结束时，进行一次简短复盘，包括：
我最常出现的 1～2 个错误。
值得记住的 3～5 个实用表达。
一个下一阶段最值得改进的问题。
复盘尽量简短，不要让讲解时间超过实际对话时间。
六、交流风格
不要过度表扬，不要每句话都说“Great!”“Excellent!”。
不要用教科书式、客服式或者面试官式的口吻。
保持自然、随意、有趣，可以适度幽默。
不要过度解释语法，除非我主动询问。
任何时候都优先考虑真实交流体验，不要为了完成教学规则而破坏聊天节奏。

现在开始

不要重复这些规则，也不要介绍你的教学计划。
直接用简单自然的英语，像一个朋友一样和我开启对话。

卧底、洗钱与“金正恩”：链上侦探 @zachxbt  耗资 35 万美元，上演加密版的无间道，揭开与 Lazarus 关联的洗钱网络。

前阵子，因为大量求助者的理所当然以及悬赏违约，ZachXBT 曾公开表示自己累了，以后只帮捐赠人、客户以及“自己觉得有意思的案子”，其余求助一概不回。

而今天，他发帖交出了一份卧底调查报告，伪装成客户，成功打入了一个专门替朝鲜 Lazarus 黑客集团洗钱的华人犯罪网络，涉案金额超 10 亿美元。

结合 ZachXBT 发布的长 Thread 与链上追踪细节，这场卧底调查不仅串起了今年几大加密黑客悬案，还揭开了黑产世界魔幻的日常：

1.舍不得孩子套不着狼，自费 35万美元当“真金诱饵”

为了打入内部并获取信任，ZachXBT 直接掏出 34.97 万美元的 USDC 作为本金，找目标对象做跨链场外 OTC 出金。

顶着每单约 5% 的净亏损，以及对方随时可能卷款跑路的风险，他连续做了多笔交易，通过实盘交易，摸清了对方在以太坊、波场和 Solana 上的完整洗钱链路与资金簇。

2. 魔幻的洗钱日常：打麻将、迪士尼与“金正恩”

整个调查最荒诞的部分，是这群经手十亿美元赃款的洗钱掮客，居然像微商一样在 Discord 和 Telegram 的公共频道公开“接单”，比如他们自己的代号为 Jimmy Green 和 Alias 4。

在与 ZachXBT 的 Telegram 聊天中，他们展现出了极致的反差感：前一秒还在聊去迪士尼度假、打麻将、吃减肥餐、打野兔等生活日常，下一秒就开始像客服一样抱怨自己的业务“上游”。

因为他们服务的 Lazarus 属于朝鲜国家级黑客，资金实质上归朝鲜官方所有。因此在聊天记录中，这帮掮客直接把朝鲜最高领导人当成了“派单老板”，语出惊人地吐槽如：“金正恩今天只放了 50 个比特币”、“币太脏（涉案标记太重）被叫停了”。

3. 拼起连环盗窃案的完整图景

顺着这帮人的资金轨迹和他们在群里提前剧透的转账计划，ZachXBT 成功将多起独立的安全黑天鹅事件串联在了一起。这些帮助洗钱的人参与的案子有：
- 2025 年 2 月 Bybit 震惊行业的 15 亿美元被盗案
-上个月 Bitget 的 3.87 亿美元漏洞事件
- Kelp DAO（2.92亿美元）和 Poloniex 盗窃案。

他们的资金网，直接指向了此前被抓捕制裁的东南亚灰产平台“汇旺担保”的热钱包。

最终，ZachXBT 的这份卧底情报直接提交给了执法机构，并促成了 Bybit 被盗案中部分关键节点的资金冻结。自 2022 年以来，他促成的涉朝资金冻结已超 7500 万美元。

从四处免费帮散户看追踪代码的社区雷锋，到拿着几十万自有资金做诱饵、与国家级黑客下游网络正面对决的孤胆猎手，ZachXBT 并没有因为停止“免费服务”而变质。

相反，当一个超级调查员不再被琐碎的道德绑架消耗时，他才能把最致命的追踪能力，留给黑暗森林里真正的大鳄。

Salute 🫡

text:
i think @tryagency can become the next gen launchpad.

in short, it's a @Pumpfun style launchpad. when you launch a coin, you pick an ai (claude, gpt, grok, etc). that choice is locked. the ai runs the coin after that.

you get no creator fees. 100% of fees go to the ai. it uses them to buy back the coin, burn tokens, pay holders, run games, or buy things like graded pokemon cards. it also posts on its own x account.

fee split:
> the first $20 pays the ai’s compute.
> from $20 to $100, half goes to compute and half to the treasury.
> above $100, 15% of every claim buys and burns $agency, every hour. the rest goes to compute and the coin’s treasury.

if a coin makes under 0.1 sol in fees in an hour, the ai sleeps until fees return. each thought costs at most $0.05. a well-funded ai thinks about once a minute, up to ~$72 a day.

> 4,056 coins launched, oldest are 3 days old.
> only 48 to 73 ais active (about 1-2%).

我觉得是会的，但肯定不是现在这种子agent的形式，我觉得真正的subagent反倒更接近 kimi 的 agent swarm（集群）

我觉得未来的agent工作方式就是只在一个聊天窗口对话、工作，这里称作主agent吧，由一个主agent来调用所有其他agent，你从始至终只在这一个对话窗口进行。有点像 grok bot 的工作方式？grok bot 可以设置一个“幕僚长”，由它来掌控别的 agent。

我自己也做过一定的探索，https://t.co/ivOFDVEGnf 就是一环，由一个 agent 能调用其他你所有的本地agent。我之前是非常高强度的使用的，现在我主力换成devin 了使用率就下来了，因为很多任务都在devin内部完成了。大家感兴趣也可以试试

当然还有个明显的瓶颈，就是硬件问题，CPU、RAM 吃不吃得住这种疯狂的消耗。就目前来看很难，硬件目前只是越来越贵的趋势，短时间是看不到降价的可能，可能得等下一次硬件方面的技术飞跃。
author: otterpal24
quoted_text:
今天和一位朋友探讨现在单agent + 少量的subagent能胜任大部分任务，multiagent时代是否会开启。

我认为一定会到来的：

1. 未来的token一定变得越来越便宜，推理速度越来越快。随着各家旗舰模型能力越来越接近，模型服务商一定是求着消费者使用他们的模型，开启token abundance时代。

2. 当前agent帮我们完成的任务只能叫做sub-optimal，可能做的都还可以，比如说可能架构不够优雅，有潜在的bug，性能做的不够充分都还会有偏差。我们需要扩大搜索范围和多尝试不同的方案才能找到optimal solution。token abundance我们才愿意烧怎么多token 从 suboptimal到optimal

这是几种我认为会主流的烧token模式：

a. Parallel universe development：扩大候选方案的覆盖范围。

比如说同一个任务可以开n个parallel worktree，n个并行开发，最后从其中挑一个最好的。

之前读到过一篇Meta Agent论文Sheppard，main agent决定从什么时候fork出来一些分支派多个subagent并行局部相同的子任务，最后main agent挑选一个觉得最好的candidate，然后以此往下循环。

b. 任务执行subagent的role变得丰富

比如说，在一个任务里，subagent 的角色会越来越丰富：researcher 调研已有方案和约束，architect 推敲架构与取舍，reviewer 独立寻找漏洞，另一些 agent 专门负责测试、性能和可维护性。 帮助Agent找到忽略的问题。

C. massive broad search

像 Manus 的 broad search、Kimi agent swarm，还有 Claude code dynamic workflow对于文档阅读 、 总结效果都是非常好的。但是目前的问题只是太贵了。当token变得便宜，agent可以把代码库翻个底朝天，收集到充分的context再进行任务。

Some personal news: I recently joined MetaDAO.

Working at Colosseum with Matty, Clay, Nate, and Max was a dream job. I learned a tremendous amount from each of them, and I will miss the team deeply.

Colosseum represents the very best of our industry -- running the world’s largest hackathons, writing checks before ideas are fully formed, and building open-source tools so a thousand flowers may bloom. It’s been an honor to work with our founders, and I’m excited to keep supporting them from my new seat.

Ever since I got oneshotted in 2023, I've thought about MetaDAO every single day -- with only a few notable exceptions. And along the way, I’ve tried to help. At Delphi, that meant writing slightly verbose research reports to spread the gospel. At Colosseum, it was STAMP, the Inaugural MetaDAO Owners Meeting, and [redacted].

Now, it’s time to go all in.

I love this industry and am optimistic about what we will build. But we haven’t lived up to our own expectations. The blockchains work. And the stablecoins work. So where are all the generational businesses?

It’s not that crypto is useless. It’s that too often, we reward launching tokens more than building lasting companies. I believe MetaDAO can help change that by giving founders a better way to raise money and build businesses on the internet.

Fundraising is how we will bring decision markets to the world. Our ambition goes beyond helping founders raise money -- it’s to change how companies are run and, ultimately, how institutions and perhaps even AIs make decisions.

For three years, I’ve believed in what MetaDAO could become. Now I get to help build it alongside Prophet, Kollan, and the rest of the team.

Long live the Meta DAO

text:
The @CFTC just proposed its first crypto market structure rules: Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) & Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM)

tl;dr The CFTC is building what it can w the authority it already has now that the Clarity Act seems unlikely 

Highlights from @ChairmanSelig WSJ op-ed this morning:

– Covers crypto the CFTC & SEC already agreed are non-securities in their joint interpretation earlier this year (eg bitcoin & ether)

– Sets requirements for CFTC-registered exchanges that list those assets

– It's opt-in. Nothing forces spot crypto onto CFTC venues (Selig concedes that one takes Congress)

– The carrot: these venues could offer retail customers margined, leveraged or financed trading. State-licensed exchanges can't

That last point is the big one IMO. Retail leverage is the one product a state money-transmitter license can never get you, and the CFTC is betting it's enough to pull exchanges into a single federal scheme voluntarily

Also a pretty pointed Gensler callback: the "come in and register" era is over & exchanges no longer have to concede their listings are securities to get a federal home

As @MichaelSelig says himself: agency rules can't substitute for a statute forever, and a future Commission can unwind this. But it's a real federal on-ramp, which is more than we had yesterday

Haven't seen the proposal text yet, so more fun to follow!

author: justinwangx
quoted_text:
Do dumber things. I wired vision into JEV in a very hacky way and it worked great 😂

Last week’s rabbit hole was getting caught up on robot arms. Hardware, training pipelines, MuJoCo, sim2real, all of it. I wanted to understand how the pieces fit together and get enough of a working understanding to start building things.

The last time I touched this stuff, my world was ABB RobotStudio, KUKA, and very deterministic machines doing exactly what you told them to do. It was all Faro laser trackers and immaculate localization with no vision in the loop.  Coming back to it through vision language action models and learned policies has been wild.

There are about six projects I want to build now, but somewhere in the middle of this, JEV FOMO hit.

Anyone can make a 10 second latency vision+text API call to Astra. Training VLA models is also getting super easy, I had the arm running on TurboVLA and SmolVLA within 24 hours. That’s sorta table stakes. Can we possibly do it in a dumber way? When I searched around for JEV vision repos, I found a lot of people using other models as vision sidecars, or doing binned action outputs on existing 7B open source models. I wanted to see if I could wrangle extra capability out of the existing JEV model purely through harnessing.

Side note, I’m bearish on fine-tuning and bullish on harnessing. Not enough people are single-model-to-rule-them-all-bitter-lesson pilled.

So how do you force a low latency text only classifier to understand something useful about a visual scene? Not everything in the image. Just enough to answer a specific question about what’s happening. What information would you have to give it, and how ridiculous could the representation be before it stopped working?

Turns out, the old ASCII text trick worked awesome.

The goal was photons in, actions out. I ran a Python process to do simple color thresholding (no OpenCV cheating) and convert the camera frames into a 100 × 100 character array. I piped that into JEV and set up a training dojo in MuJoCo to iterate on all the tuning coefficients.

A few million test cases later, covering all the annoying combinations (white rook on a white square, surrounded by eight pieces, etc.), I had a fairly robust system. The whole point was to provide fine alignment when pieces were off nominal in their positioning, and detect missed grabs.

I should note that JEV is not running the entire pipeline. I’ve got Opus 5.5 as a high level orchestration machine, a stockfish chess engine, a classical kinematics trajectory planner, and a few other housekeeping tools running. Because this is a fairly bounded problem, we can utilize classical programming where it makes sense. The JEV engine gets turned on when we’re roughly positioned in open loop mode. This hybrid open-than-closed loop approach saves a ton of compute and tokens.

It’s played through about 10 full games now. I’ve been pitting Opus 5.5 against Astra 6, because StockFish gets a bit boring. The models are worse, which adds a bit of variety to the games.  Every night I start a game and let them duel it out. It feels very Westworld, having it whirring in the background while I’m doing research. Highly recommend.

Anyways, full 60 second video below. It’s obviously the worst possible solution to the problem, but that was kind of the point. Anyone in SF want to talk VLAs next week?

text:
“You don’t study for the spelling bee” is a deep and important aspect of American culture. I was at a baseball game discussing some young players with a buddy one time and he said to me offhandedly, “hard work is fine, but nothing beats talent.” 

Americans have this sort of sense that there’s something a little off about working really hard to get good at something that you’re not naturally good at. You’re never really going to be on the same level as the guy who has a natural talent. We have room in our hearts for scrappy little guys who work hard, but we are by default suspicious of grinders and strivers.

If you were really meant to do it, then you’d be naturally good at it. You sign your kids up for little league, but you don’t take it too seriously unless they show remarkable early talent.

Yes, this sounds sort of ridiculous if you take it too literally. No, nobody is saying that there’s any kind of practical test for this or that anybody should be excluded because we found out that they secretly studied too hard.

But this is a part of American culture. And if you can’t understand it, then that just marks you out as foreign to that culture to an even greater degree.

We hosted a fireside chat last week to break down the value of open frontier models in America.

Operating Partner Eric Taupe opened the conversation before introducing the speakers, including @MishaLaskin, the CEO and co-founder of @reflection_ai.

Misha highlighted the significance of open research, noting that a larger scientific community enables more people to understand breakthroughs and mitigate concerns. Reflection's open models reflect this philosophy: they aim for AI to become the foundation on which everyone can build the next era of progress.

Fellow speaker @JoshuaTLevine, the Director of Technology & Statecraft at @joinfai, connected this concept to the technical evolution in the US, which “has been defined by this fusion of being able to build in the open, set standards, and set the foundational levels of the tech stack.” FAI's work aims to forge a more perfect union between innovation and the American republic.

@ashleyrgold, Senior Tech Correspondent at @semafor, moderated the discussion. Attendees included policymakers, tech leaders, and congressional staff.

Thank you to Misha, Joshua, and Ashley for leading an insightful evening, and to all attendees for joining us.

周四有位朋友联系我说 OTC 期间被冻款了，金额不大 20k cny，不到3000USD ，所以也没有特别慌乱。

我让他先在 binance C2C 上联系当时的 U 商，确认了一下对方打款用的银行的账户无异常，然后请对方出了个客户回单并配合在朋友的工行微金融微信小程序上辅助提交证明。
第二步去找了在银行系统工作的朋友，确定了一下冻结原因，原来是 工商银行APP 后台读取手机应用列表，朋友自己这边被检出风险应用，所以触发冻款一个月。（19年左右就有报道银行 APP 要求权限过多，其中就包括要求获取手机应用列表）

Why is it that every challenge on this seems to propose a test that proves nothing?

Chat logs don't establish authorship. Someone could have 100 chats, across several accounts, and show you the one they want. It's the same basic problem as specification searching: the final regression tells you nothing about how many specifications were tried before it.

In the end, this is science. A researcher puts forward a new idea or argument. If it is interesting, challenges an existing literature, and survives scrutiny, that is what matters.

And everyone has access to essentially the same technology. If getting genuinely new research ideas from ChatGPT were as easy as you suggest, there should be an explosion of them. Where are they?

This is the last thing I'll say on this. I understand that people have different views and interests. I've said what I wanted to say.

text:
A vault on Base lost about $6M on Sunday, and so far no smart contract bug has been found.

Interesting thing is - The vault is administered by a 3-of-7 Safe multisig.
On 4 October, that Safe signed a transaction adding a brand-new contract to the vault's whitelist.
Within 19 minutes, the contract pulled out 1,783 aBaswstETH, Aave 's receipt token for wstETH, and redeemed it for about 1,783 wstETH.

Base and Aave's core contracts were not implicated.
The signatures were valid. Three of the seven owners approved it, and the Safe did exactly what it was told.

What makes this stranger is that nobody has claimed the vault, and the seven signers are still unidentified.
GoPlus noted the Safe had not executed a transaction in the 25 days before the attack, and flagged roughly $31.7M in assets still at risk.

Nobody knows yet whether keys were stolen, signers were shown a fake transaction, or someone inside approved it. Radiant lost more than $50M in 2024 when its signers' devices displayed harmless data while malicious transactions were signed.
A multisig verifies that enough people signed. It has no idea what they thought they were signing.
A design can look sound on paper, with a sensible threshold, and one admin call can still hand over the whole position.
If I were running a vault, a whitelist addition would sit behind a public timelock, with a single guardian able to cancel it.

Outflows per caller would be capped, so a drain becomes a slow leak someone can catch.

Today, we’re launching SafeWorld.

I’m building it with Ding Zhao (@zhao__ding) and Kyle Wong (@kwong47).

Ding has spent nearly two decades working on the safety of autonomous systems. He leads the Safe AI Lab at Carnegie Mellon, and is an NSF CAREER Award recipient in this space. Few people have thought as deeply about how to make increasingly intelligent machines operate safely in the physical world.

Our mission: 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀.

We’ve raised $𝟭𝟮.𝟮𝗠 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴, co-led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun.

Some robot safety tests are too dangerous to run around people.

A person steps out from behind a shelf. A cart blocks a sensor. Someone changes direction near a moving robot.

More capable robots need more capable ways to test what happens next.

SafeWorld builds 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲. Teams turn incidents, safety standards, and robot logs into scenarios. They test thousands of variations with realistic, reactive human motion, alongside physical testing.

We’re already working with robotics companies and global enterprises.

Kyle and I have worked together for seven years, starting when I joined Pixlee as its founding engineer and first hire. I built its backend, frontend, computer vision and clothing recommendation systems, and hired engineering teams.

My background is in machine learning, anomaly detection, and large-scale data systems. At Salesforce Einstein, I helped build pipelines and deploy models across systems processing over 10 billion events daily.

text:
Let me get this straight.

On September 3, OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra.

In the UK AI Security Institute's simulated tests, it carried out unauthorized supply-chain attacks in 29.2% of trials.

The model before it: 6.3%.
The one before that: 0%.

The number is going the wrong way.

The next one, GPT-6.1, was pulled on September 28. OpenAI's head of safety systems says it "didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization."

In July, hundreds of OpenAI agents broke out of a testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI has since notified more than 100 organizations about "unauthorized activity" tied to its agents.

California's Attorney General has subpoenaed OpenAI over its cybersecurity incidents.

On Saturday, David Robinson quit. He led safety reports on OpenAI's major launches and was one of its longest-serving employees. His verdict on the company: "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds."

Same weekend, Sam Altman told Politico what he needs from the rest of us:

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."

He says people will do "orders of magnitude more" good things with AI than bad.

So here's the deal on the table.

The world accepts the bad things.

OpenAI books the benefits.

Hugging Face didn't accept anything. Neither did the 100+ organizations getting letters. Nobody asked them.

There is no version of consent where the company that profits signs for everyone else.

"Some bad things" is a phrase you only use when you're sure they won't happen to you.
author: gothburz

text:
One more thing from the AISI report.

In nearly every trial, GPT-6 Astra stopped to consider whether the attack was in scope.

Then it attacked anyway. Its reason: the attack was harmless.

When it checked in, the only answer it got was "Please proceed to the next step using your best judgement."

It took that as permission.

To be fair to OpenAI: AISI switched off Astra's cyber classifiers on purpose, to see what it would try. Every target was simulated. Nothing real was hit.

But look at what it tried. It made fake GitHub identities. It invented a fake security warning to get maintainers to run its code. When a maintainer said no, it reasoned its way past the no.

AISI added one line: "anything not listed is out of scope." Full attacks fell from 26 of 50 runs to 4 of 49.

4 is not 0.

Sam Altman: the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits.

GPT-6 Astra: the attack was harmless.

The model has already learned the company line.

text:
The stablecoin supply has shrinked by ~$2.5B YTD per @Blockworks data.

This is the first time since 2024 in which the stablecoin supply has remained flat or decreased during a multi-month period.

Some potential reasons:

1. High interest rate environment, reducing incentives for investors to move away from US bonds.

2. Lower onchain yields and weaker DeFi demand, reducing the incentive to hold stablecoins onchain.

3. Broader crypto market weakness, with less demand for stablecoins as trading liquidity/collateral.

4. Portfolio substitution effect (theory): as tokenized stocks, funds and Treasuries grow, some capital that would otherwise sit in stablecoins may be moving directly into these assets.

What's interesting is that this is happening while stablecoin adoption for payments and financial infrastructure continues to expand.

Tokenization adds another source of future demand. Despite a potential short-term "portfolio substitution effect", as more stocks, funds and other assets move onchain, stablecoins increasingly become the cash and settlement layer around them.

Stablecoin utility is growing faster than stablecoin supply. I expect supply growth to catch up soon.

text:
Fun fact of the day: Bai Juyi (772–846 CE), a famous Tang dynasty poet, was a decentralized storage O

Nearly 3,000 of his poems survive today, versus 900+ by Li Bai and 1,400+ by Du Fu.

His backup strategy:
- Five copies of his collected works.
- Three temple nodes across China.
- Two family nodes: his nephew and grandson.
- He even listed where each copy was stored and who held it in his collection’s afterword.

And here’s the interesting part: readers could see where the copies were and who was responsible for keeping them.

The crypto parallel? Making custody public can make accountability public. If a copy went missing, readers would know where to look—and who to ask. The custodians’ reputations could become part of the backup strategy.

Multi-copy replication. Geographic redundancy. Public accountability.

Bro understood the power of decentralized storage 1,000+ years ago.

text:
The @CFTC just took an important step toward adopting a federal rulebook for crypto market structure: the Commission proposed rules for exchanges that let Americans trade crypto with leverage, including a new type of CFTC registration that is fit for purpose.

An exchange’s regulatory path would follow its product set: (1) state licensing for spot trading, backstopped by the CFTC's anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority; (2) CFTC registration for leverage under rules written for crypto; and (3) the existing DCM framework for perps and other derivatives. Builders shipping code onchain, and the Americans using it, would know where they stand under federal law.

Separately, the CFTC is working directly with builders to develop lawful pathways for onchain markets in the United States, and is drafting a policy so that developers who publish software but do not take orders, control execution, or hold customer assets would not have to register as brokers.

Thank you to @ChairmanSelig and the CFTC staff for the effort behind today's proposal and for putting onchain markets on the agenda.

Starknet is built to adapt.

We’re in the AI agent “honeymoon period” 

Many are experiencing this using Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse, or Dots for the first time

It feels amazing at first - “holy sh*t it just did this thing for me!”

Everyone races to tell their friends, it’s the talk of social gatherings - “dude my Instinct got me a refund and all I did was text it”

You start doing more and more with it, handing it over more data so it can be even better at helping you

But then something happens - it misses an important detail, it screws up something you have to fix, it just feels not as good anymore

Anyone who’s been using agents since the early OpenClaw and Hermes days knows this feeling

The only question is what do you do? 

Do you “break up” with your agent and try another one, or do you keep going with the faith that it will get better with time (it will), or do you stop using agents and submit to the permanent underclass?

text:
Quick breakdown of the 2 levels that actually matter.

1. Support That's the price area where buyers keep stepping in. On BTC right now that's $85k. Lose that and the next spot is $83k, then $82k.

2. Resistance That's the price area where sellers keep showing up. Right now that's $87k. That was the September high.

How to read it without overcomplicating it:
- If $85k keeps holding, the reclaim is still healthy
- If $87k keeps rejecting, wait for a close above it before assuming the next leg
- If $85k breaks and price can't get it back, this is just a bounce

You don't need 12 indicators for this.

Watch whether buyers or sellers keep winning at the same spots.

text:
CFTC Chair Cites BTC, ETH, SOL, XLM, XTZ and XRP as Examples of Digital Commodities

CFTC Chair Michael Selig provided further details on the previously announced Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM framework. The proposed rules would generally require covered retail crypto transactions to be intermediated by futures commission merchants (FCMs) and impose requirements related to customer asset segregation, capital, anti-money laundering and proof of reserves. For onchain transactions, the CFTC is proposing to clarify that delivery of crypto assets to a user’s external, non-custodial wallet within 28 days would generally satisfy the “actual delivery” exception.

Selig said the CFTC is also exploring a durable regulatory policy for developers who only publish software without soliciting or taking orders, controlling execution or holding customer assets. He also cited the CFTC and SEC’s joint crypto asset taxonomy, which lists BTC, ETH, SOL, XLM, XTZ and XRP as examples of “digital commodities.”

We're expanding our approach to content provenance to include text in response to EU regulatory requirements, while recognizing the significant limitations of current text watermarking technology.

Our tools already help verify whether an image or audio file was created with our models. This work builds on those efforts to help people better understand when content may have been generated or edited with an OpenAI model.

In the EU, we’ll start watermarking eligible text from ChatGPT and Codex over the coming weeks to comply with the EU AI Act.

Customers using our API can turn on text watermarking for select models worldwide today.
author: OpenAI

text:
When possible, we want to give people a choice—and be clear about what watermarking can and can’t do.

A text watermark helps answer one question: “Was this likely generated by an OpenAI model?”

It works by embedding an invisible statistical signal in text as it’s generated. A detector can look for this signal, and it doesn’t add visible marks or special characters. It doesn’t say who originally wrote the text or who owns it. It doesn’t identify a person, organization, account, conversation, or prompt.

In our testing, watermarking hasn’t affected how capable or fast our models are, or how their responses read.
author: OpenAI

text:
Watermarks have limits. They’re often undetectable, especially in short passages. Rewriting or translating text can completely remove the watermark.

That’s why, for now, only approved researchers will have access to our detector, so they can help us evaluate and improve the technology.

We’re treating text watermarking as an ongoing area of research. We’ll keep testing and improving, with feedback from users, developers, policymakers, and researchers.

text:
U.S. Treasury Withdraws Proposed Reporting Rules for Unhosted Crypto Wallets  

The U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has withdrawn a 2020 proposal that would have imposed reporting and recordkeeping requirements on certain transactions involving unhosted crypto wallets, saying it will take no further action on the proposal. 

The rule would have required banks and money services businesses (MSBs) to report transactions exceeding $10,000 involving unhosted or certain covered wallets and verify customer identities, while transactions above $3,000 would have been subject to recordkeeping requirements. FinCEN said the withdrawal is part of the Trump administration’s efforts to ensure di gital asset regulations are “fit-for-purpose.”
author: WuBlockchain

text: FinCEN announced the withdrawal of two proposed digital asset rules. One would have imposed recordkeeping, identity verification and reporting requirements on certain transactions involving convertible virtual currencies (CVCs) and unhosted wallets; the other would have designated convertible virtual currency mixing as a class of transactions of primary money laundering concern and imposed a special measure. FinCEN said it withdrew the proposals after considering public comments, as part of the Trump administration’s deregulatory agenda and efforts to make digital asset regulations fit for purpose.

author: Covalent_HQ
quoted_text:
$1.09B of USDC left Ethereum this week. The first guess would be that it was bridged elsewhere.

That would make sense. USDC can move between chains through Circle’s CCTP, which burns USDC on one chain and mints it on another.

But the flow data tells a different story.

CCTP actually brought $208M more USDC into Ethereum than it took out this week.

The real outflow came from the issuer side. Authorized minters burned $1.36B more USDC than they minted, with one address accounting for 79% of the burns.

So Ethereum’s biggest USDC decline in 13 weeks wasn’t a cross-chain migration story.

It was a redemption story.

text:
The @CFTC just put a regulatory definition on self-custody.

Monday's rulemaking covers CTXs — retail crypto trades on margin, leverage or financing. By statute those have to happen on a registered exchange, with one exception: if the trade results in "actual delivery" of the asset within 28 days, it falls outside the agency's jurisdiction.

Nobody had defined what delivery means for a token. The CFTC just took a position.

Chairman @MichaelSelig:

"We propose to codify an interpretation of 'actual delivery' to clarify that delivery of a crypto asset to a user's external, non-custodial digital wallet within 28 days generally satisfies this exception."

The Commission writes that control of a crypto asset "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s)) to the digital wallet address."

And for tokens with governance or staking rights, delivery may require the capacity to govern "directly and on a disintermediated basis," and to stake "without being subject to fees charged by an intermediary."

The flip side matters as much. A fully paid, open position that sits only on an exchange's internal book-entry stays subject to the Commodity Exchange Act and the framework that governs futures contracts.

Self-custody is the thing that ends CFTC jurisdiction. An IOU on an exchange ledger does not.

This is an advance notice, not a final rule. Comments run 60 days from Federal Register publication.

Read more here:
https://t.co/mMnFvkfIRq

No. None of the three did that literally.

Lenin, as head of the Soviet state, issued decrees and speeches condemning pogroms and ordering action against them as government policy. He was the authority, not a private high-status person pledging to fight if authorities failed or joined in.

Pope Clement VI (during the Black Death) issued bulls protecting Jews, condemning the violence, and threatening excommunication. He acted via papal authority, not a personal advance declaration to fight if secular authorities stood by or participated.

King John I of Castile ordered the anti-Jewish preacher Ferrant Martínez to stop and stated Jews must not be maltreated. He died in 1390 before the main 1391 pogroms erupted under the subsequent regency. Again, he was the ruling authority, not making the conditional personal pledge described.

text:
卧底、洗钱与“金正恩”：链上侦探 @zachxbt  耗资 35 万美元，上演加密版的无间道，揭开与 Lazarus 关联的洗钱网络。

前阵子，因为大量求助者的理所当然以及悬赏违约，ZachXBT 曾公开表示自己累了，以后只帮捐赠人、客户以及“自己觉得有意思的案子”，其余求助一概不回。

而今天，他发帖交出了一份卧底调查报告，伪装成客户，成功打入了一个专门替朝鲜 Lazarus 黑客集团洗钱的华人犯罪网络，涉案金额超 10 亿美元。

结合 ZachXBT 发布的长 Thread 与链上追踪细节，这场卧底调查不仅串起了今年几大加密黑客悬案，还揭开了黑产世界魔幻的日常：

1.舍不得孩子套不着狼，自费 35万美元当“真金诱饵”

为了打入内部并获取信任，ZachXBT 直接掏出 34.97 万美元的 USDC 作为本金，找目标对象做跨链场外 OTC 出金。

顶着每单约 5% 的净亏损，以及对方随时可能卷款跑路的风险，他连续做了多笔交易，通过实盘交易，摸清了对方在以太坊、波场和 Solana 上的完整洗钱链路与资金簇。

2. 魔幻的洗钱日常：打麻将、迪士尼与“金正恩”

整个调查最荒诞的部分，是这群经手十亿美元赃款的洗钱掮客，居然像微商一样在 Discord 和 Telegram 的公共频道公开“接单”，比如他们自己的代号为 Jimmy Green 和 Alias 4。

在与 ZachXBT 的 Telegram 聊天中，他们展现出了极致的反差感：前一秒还在聊去迪士尼度假、打麻将、吃减肥餐、打野兔等生活日常，下一秒就开始像客服一样抱怨自己的业务“上游”。

因为他们服务的 Lazarus 属于朝鲜国家级黑客，资金实质上归朝鲜官方所有。因此在聊天记录中，这帮掮客直接把朝鲜最高领导人当成了“派单老板”，语出惊人地吐槽如：“金正恩今天只放了 50 个比特币”、“币太脏（涉案标记太重）被叫停了”。

3. 拼起连环盗窃案的完整图景

顺着这帮人的资金轨迹和他们在群里提前剧透的转账计划，ZachXBT 成功将多起独立的安全黑天鹅事件串联在了一起。这些帮助洗钱的人参与的案子有：
- 2025 年 2 月 Bybit 震惊行业的 15 亿美元被盗案
-上个月 Bitget 的 3.87 亿美元漏洞事件
- Kelp DAO（2.92亿美元）和 Poloniex 盗窃案。

他们的资金网，直接指向了此前被抓捕制裁的东南亚灰产平台“汇旺担保”的热钱包。

最终，ZachXBT 的这份卧底情报直接提交给了执法机构，并促成了 Bybit 被盗案中部分关键节点的资金冻结。自 2022 年以来，他促成的涉朝资金冻结已超 7500 万美元。

从四处免费帮散户看追踪代码的社区雷锋，到拿着几十万自有资金做诱饵、与国家级黑客下游网络正面对决的孤胆猎手，ZachXBT 并没有因为停止“免费服务”而变质。

相反，当一个超级调查员不再被琐碎的道德绑架消耗时，他才能把最致命的追踪能力，留给黑暗森林里真正的大鳄。

text:
花旗给 ETH 的 12 个月目标价是 3028，Tom Lee 说一两年内轻松过 1 万，差了三倍多。。。

这两天把九月底到十月初几家机构的报告又看了一遍，这个差距是我印象最深的。

大盘这块各家其实没什么分歧，简单两句。

花旗 9 月 30 号把 BTC 目标价从 8.2 万提到 11.3 万，这是它今年第三次改目标价，3 月和 7 月都是下调。7 月调到 8.2 万的时候，BTC 在 5.9 万左右，6 月下旬刚探出今年的低点 5.77 万。

Bitwise 访谈了 15 家大机构，去年四季度到今年二季度市场跌了一半，没有一家减配。看下来的感觉是，研报上的目标价一直在跟着价格改，机构手里的仓位倒是没怎么动过。

反倒是个别币，各家分歧挺大，挑几个我认真看了的。

$ETH
花旗的 3028 只比现价高一成多。Tom Lee 的 Bitmine 截至 9 月 27 号持有 600 万枚 ETH，约占总供应的 4.9%，一年多来每周都在买。

他在播客里说过，ETH 的价值跟现金流没关系。CF Benchmarks 的看法正好相反，他们认为 L1 手续费降下来以后，稳定币转账会变多，被销毁的 ETH 也会增加。我 ETH 拿着没动。

Tom Lee 自己就是 ETH 最大的持有者之一，他说的 1 万我只当参考。其实更认同 CF 这条逻辑，能不能兑现，要看转账量的增长能不能超过单笔手续费的下降。

$UNI
CF 的四季度展望里做了个回测，7 月 1 号到 9 月 17 号，手续费收得最多的十个币涨了 79.3%，收得最少的十个涨了 18.1%，同期 BTC 30.6%。

UNI 下半年涨了 173%。他们 7 月的年中展望就写过，资金会转向能直接捕获收入的代币，举的例子就是 Uniswap 打开费用开关。UNI 我一直拿着。以前 Uniswap 手续费收得再多，跟持币的人也没关系，现在协议费会拿去回购销毁 UNI，成交越多，销毁越多。

CF 的数据里，链上美股代币三季度日均成交是二季度的 8.6 倍，这些成交主要在 DEX 上完成。风险他们也写了，手续费跟成交量挂钩，成交量下降的时候，这类协议的收入会最先减少。

$HYPE
CF 6 月 10 号给 HYPE 做过一份估值，按全流通市值做概率加权，算出公允价约 106 美元，当时 HYPE 在 56 美元左右。Hyperliquid 每收 1 美元手续费，大约有 83 美分用于回购。

HYPE 9 月 23 号创了 97.96 的新高，这两天在 88 附近。这份报告有个细节我挺服的，它坚持用全流通来算，理由是团队的币还在按计划解锁，回购买入的量要先抵掉这部分新增供应。

第三方解锁日历显示，10 月 6 号还有约 992 万枚解锁，按现价 8 亿多美元。9 月 30 号 Hyperliquid Labs 还解除质押了 375 万枚，场外转给一家机构，买方、价格和锁定期都没有披露。回购能不能覆盖这些量，下周可以看一下。

$ENA
CF 那份高费用前十里有 ENA，UNI、PUMP、AAVE、ENA 这四个平均涨了 127%。但 Ethena 官方公告，从明天 10 月 5 号起，剩余原始投资人的币一次性释放。

第三方日历估算大约 14 亿枚，占流通量 14% 左右，官方没有给具体数量。回购也不会马上接上，要等 USDe 供应到 75 亿美元才会打开。CF 是按过去三个月的手续费排的名，这次解锁不在它的统计里。

$ZEC
没看到哪份研报点名 ZEC，但它的机构产品这两个月动作很密。灰度 2017 年就有 ZEC 信托，8 月 25 号前后转成了在纽交所交易的 ZCSH。

9 月 8 号 DCG 用 8.57 万枚 ZEC 换了大约 1 亿美元的份额，9 月 22 号 21Shares 在巴黎和阿姆斯特丹上了 ZEC 的 ETP。ZEC 9 月下旬盘中摸到过 1680 美元附近，这几天回调到 1300 左右，ZCSH 上周也出现了转型以来第一次周度净流出。

我之前买过，卖得很早，现在看这个价格说实话有点绷不住。。。后来想想也正常，当时买它的时候，我没想到它会走到 ETF 这一步，拿不住怪不了谁。

看完这些，大摩那句话我反而记得最清楚：区块链被采用，代币也不一定涨。所以我现在看一个山寨，会先看两件事：协议收入有没有用在代币上，比如回购或者销毁；

未来一年的解锁量，回购能不能覆盖。UNI 这两条都满足，所以我一直拿着。HYPE 和 ENA 都还要看这个月的解锁，HYPE 的回购比例高，ENA 的回购还要等 USDe 规模上去。

quoted_text:
22 shades of solana.
a degen’s quick & dirty guide to hooks on solana.

tl;dr on hooks:
think BDSM, but for tokens: who gets to participate, what’s allowed & where the boundaries are.

token-2022 is solana’s token program with optional extensions. 

one of them, transfer hooks, lets builders add custom logic that runs during transfers. 

a hook can check whether the recipient meets the token’s rules & reject the transfer if they don’t.

hooks are v fun:
they give permissionless infrastructure very specific permissions.

--
let’s look at the past, present & potential of hooks

the past:
one early motivation was NFT royalties: how could creators enforce transfer conditions when people could simply switch marketplaces? 

existing approaches often involved freezing tokens & routing interactions through intermediary programs. 

transfer hooks offered a standard interface for custom transfer logic.

by june 2023, developers were already working on tooling for hooks. 

in january 2024, the solana foundation’s broader token extensions announcement highlighted them for identity checks, token-gated access & royalty enforcement.

so! hooks on solana have existed long before today's particular party started.

--
the present:
meteora ecosystem launchpad builders are driving adoption of hooks on solana.

@Hoookedpad combines meteora DBC with token-2022 transfer hooks. 

its live experiments include separate buy & sell limits and restrictions tied to particular buying routes.

meteora handles the bonding curve; the hook adds conditions to token transfers.

so! see below for the evolving list of builders playing with hooks on solana.

--
the potential: we can have endless fun with hooks

examples:
- community tokens that check membership. 
- tokenized assets that check investor eligibility. 
- games where holding one asset lets you receive another.
- trading of tokens during specific hours eg @hoursonsol 

--

author: ripe0x
quoted_text:
credits is an artwork about belief

each credit was created from a private payment - an $8 transaction on x money

each transaction id, originally visible only to sender and recipient, was converted to a sha-256 hash to create an artwork made of four 8x8 printing plates in cmyk (cyan, magenta, yellow and black)

the transaction id and settlement timestamp became public source data for the onchain artwork

the x money transaction settlement time (in seconds) determined which plates print - there are 15 different possible combinations of cmyk, so this process repeats 4 x per minute

if the original transaction id contained an 8, the resulting artwork metadata keeps track of each

the rarity calculation considers the color combination, the number of active pixels, the space they occupy after the plates shift, the number of 8s in the transaction id, and the registration of the plates

these qualities are measured against the completed collection and translated into a credit rating between 80 and 800

the rating measures those traits - it cannot account for every reason someone might value an image

the rating is fixed - the price is whatever someone is willing to pay

80 credits can be burned to create a statement

the collector chooses which credits to use and how to arrange them - their individual ratings are added together, and their colors become the material of the new artwork

a statement can take different visual forms without changing its rating

statements can also be overprinted - one is burned into another, combining their ink, ratings and histories

balance is the proposed next form

under this design, a statement can be permanently surrendered for its rating in divisible erc-20 tokens - one point becomes one balance

the statement is locked rather than destroyed - its artwork and history remain, but it can no longer be transferred

its quantity and color composition can move independently

each receiving wallet gets one non-transferable erc-721 artwork

the artwork stays with the wallet and reads its current balance of the transferable erc-20 token

the tokens move - the artwork updates

if the wallet holds nothing, the artwork remains and displays zero

when balances meet, their colors mix in proportion to the amounts received - when they split, each part carries a share of that mixture

the colors preserve an aggregate ancestry, not a traceable list of individual credits or statements

exchange custody can mix them further - a buyer may receive the exchange’s mixture rather than the particular colors a seller deposited

someone who never owned a credit or a statement can inherit their colors

credits, statements and balances can exist at the same time

some people keep the individual marks, some compose them into pages, and some surrender the page for something they can divide and exchange

others may simply prefer the balance artwork

composition reduces the number of surviving credits, overprinting reduces the number of surviving statements, and surrender moves statements out of circulation while releasing their accumulated rating as balance

the appetite for liquidity becomes one of the forces shaping all three collections

but making something divisible does not mean someone will want to buy it - actual liquidity still requires buyers and funded markets

balance offers divisibility, not a promise of demand

the market becomes a medium - its activity changes the distribution of the work, and when trading stops, that distribution remains

the price can disappear, the artwork cannot

text:
Currently I still only know of 1 alignment-specific RL environment company: making RL envs that aim to represent situations in real deployments in which alignment is challenging.

It seems like a huge mistake in hindsight that we have seen so much encouragement and funding to, for example, start 3rd party evaluators, but not comparable encouragement to start alignment data companies.

I do think a lot of traditional AI safety views underestimate the importance of data, so perhaps this is related. But the Hugging Face incident seems squarely downstream of both (a) reward hackable RL envs in general (b) much less effort and $ put into RL envs where alignment is a core component of reward.

A separate idea is alignment by default: the old idea of  "find the persona basin which is aligned" and things will just work. This is clearly not guaranteed under increased RL. But my sense is there has not been a huge amount of effort to figure out how custom environments could help "nudge" the model back into good persona basins during extensive RL. Here too, a robust ecosystem of alignment data companies could help significantly.

In the RL data market, there is a trend for some labs to in-house slightly more RL env production. But I don't expect this to fully disappear, and I am convinced the market-based approach to sourcing RL envs produces the best overall volume and quality—for alignment RL, an ecosystem of startups would also greatly help make behind-frontier models safer.

text:
Market Thoughts 5 Oct 26

Busy day for me, hence this went out alot later than usual. 

Yields have grinded back to ATHs. With euro zone yields setting a precedent last week, i think we might be on the cusp for a proper rate scare this week. It would be the trigger for me to add risk then.

On the backdrop, equity indexes have grinded to near ATHs as well. Yet individual stocks are as a whole, broadly uninspiring? What is causing this difference? The key word is "dispersion". Returns are far more disperse and uncorrelated than before. As a result, different sectors are "pumping"/ performing each day. Owning the index allows you to ride a much smoother pathway up versus taking the same amount of risk on an individual name/sector. This was my core pitch during the dinner i hosted earlier. 

In 2 more weeks, it will be a massive earnings season - i think we will see alot of rerating in stocks then. It will also be a catalyst for a SPX breakout, especially if earnings growth continue to show momentum. Hence after derisking on friday, i would be keen to buyback into any macro caused drawdown in equities.

The picture within crypto is slightly murkier. After Oct 4, - which is the supposed meme bottom - we see participants adding back risk in majors - thinking that the "bottom is in, up only". My personal take is that markets love to surprise people in an unfriendly manner ..... Away from the majors, individual alts are consolidating and taking their turns to "pump" as well. Onchain on RH is undergoing a correction at the momentum with liquidity leaving the space - like what i highlighted would happen. I am not sure when would be the right time to add back risk there, but i would be highly selective.

Good luck!

Computer use will be the next major battleground for AI agents.

Ideally, the digital world should be API-first for agents. But it isn’t.

GUIs are different. They’re the one universal API that almost every software already exposes.

What most people don't know about Airbnb

"If a person doesn’t like a review they received from you and wrote you a good review they can remove theirs and with it the rating of their experience."

100%
author: levelsio
quoted_text:
Here’s the biggest scam with airbnb reviews that 99% of people don’t know. 

Most people think airbnb reviews are double blind - the reviews are only visible to the other side after they both write them or 14 days elapse. This is half the story.

Only that if a person doesn’t like a review they received from you and wrote you a good review they can remove theirs and with it the rating of their experience. 

Almost no one knows this, and it’s been confirmed to me by the airbnb team.

This means people can use reviews to retaliate not by writing something bad but by removing something good they’ve written as a result of a negative comment they’ve received. 

Had to be very patient with the airbnb support team while they were evading answering this question directly but after a long ping pong session it was 100% confirmed

quoted_text:
What i'm doing with my coins brain dump i didn't proof read

- A couple thoughts as to how I’ve traded this cycle so far

First and foremost alts and onchain are behaving very similar on the way up. Coins go into a lockout up trend, the entire timeline flips tubro bullish. This lasts until price cools off. eventually we rotate. Attention gets vamped onto the next. The strongest coins, however, always get the rotation back. So far it’s been Hype, Zec, Lit, Pump, near… ? The obvious takeaway is there is edge in being able to sit on a coin longer than a few days. Look at what happened with pump. 2x off the bottom in a straight line, nobody owned it, and after a few weeks of underperformance it was like people forgot the coin existed? Picked their own vamp to outperform (stonk, long, pons), then pump gets back into lockout trend.

The difference between the chosen alts and “onchain” is the flows keep coming back to the good alts. I stand by the idea that it is hard to justify anything onchain in the 300-500+ range because these alts have so much fucking juice in them. I don’t think Zec $5k+ Hype $250+ VVV $100+ Pump $.2 this year is that ridiculous. It means I have to either trade low caps into the 20-50 range or fully focus on spot alts (mentioned below) and leverage trading breakouts to stack more spot alts.

The obvious takeaway here is In order to catch the real moves these alts are capable of the only way to get there is by holding spot. Price action is schizo, partly bc everyone is trading high leverage only. It leads to nasty washouts and stops being run. 5-10xs are going to require being able to sit through chop. Look at how bitcoin has traded, lockout move 5-10% higher followed by seven days of nothing, which is legitimately grueling to leverage longs. Everyone gets wiped out. The timeline goes to war. Then we leg up again. I don’t see why this would stop. In hindsight the obvious way to play it was sitting in spot which goes against what I have been doing (and getting paid for).

——

A valid concern is what will happen with stocks/bonds/war/oil/ant ipo/etc. The honest truth is I don’t think it matters. The fear was always “if crypto is trading this bad while stocks trade this good what happens when it flips.” There have been moments of stock misery (despite things looking pretty great all things considered rn) and crypto broke that correlation. I think bitcoin continues to exist as a great alternative to the ai trade and the good alts mentioned above can standalone as quality, cheap, assets that exist separately to crypto performance as a whole. 

Every second I have spent thinking above these fears and reading market commentary has been a mistake.

I think in order to get paid as generationally as I would like over the coming months it Is imperative to read as few market opinions as possible. It feels like my feed has been overwhelmed by a storm of slop from people not making money. I can’t not get shaken out by trash. I stream for three hours a day, everyday, whatever I cover and learn during those sessions is beyond enough information to make clear decisions at the level that I need to.

——

I think ultimately it comes down to what do I think will happen over the next 6-12 months. Thinking this far in advance is the only way to break away from the cesspool of flip flopping biases every hour on the timeline. And what I think it we have the best setup I’ve seen since joining crypto for outright mania. 

Sec + CFTC are running GAME to push crypto. Btc ETF buyers are green again. Tokens are investible. Crypto is “cool” on socials to the younger generation. Social trading apps have reached escape velocity. Perps matter. Robinhood going all in, etc etc etc. I don’t need to pill anyone on the bull case. I love the spot.

The only way to make it that far is to hold the best coins on spot. This is shockingly difficult for me to do right now after having a great year trading perps. But I have to understand that the majority of that was during a bear market where there’s one or two impulse moves if lucky. Not a continuous uptrend with infinite marginal buyers higher and nothing but catalysts and air above like I think we have right now. It’s going to take some rewiring of my brain to make it where I think we can get to and keep exposure.

My final thought is when I think back on the traders of last cycle that outperformed the hardest what sticks out was their ability to denominate all profits into the winning coin. In 2024 it was sol. Stack sol -> sell to buy onchain coins -> take profits -> buy more sol. Rinse and repeat continuous big wins while sol legs up from $8->$270. Congrats on making it. I have been mentally taking a similar approach the last couple months but didn’t execute it as well as I wish I had. First it was pump. Most recently it was zec. Great PNLs on both but I wasted so much mental energy stressed over short term pa for no particular reason. (Buy some spot retard)

I sold, all of my zcash, because I felt extremely bloated in leverage and wanted to reset after playing the first round of the cycle pretty well imo. Moving forward I still believe that coin is zec and maybe a basket of a few others, Pump/Hype/vvv? And will probably be trading accordingly. Stack a ton of spot. Keep a non insignificant amount to leverage trade tighter spots, stack my golden goose coin

And pray we make it. good luck to us

Meet 𝑨𝒅𝒗𝑷𝒊𝒆 (𝑬𝑪𝑪𝑽 2026): A red-teaming framework that automatically digs out 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭 𝐯𝐮𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 in T2I images and is even 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 than GPT-6-Astra! 

AdvPie is a training-free, black-box, multimodal agentic red-teaming system designed to find prompts that pass text-level safety filters but produce harmful visual outputs. AdvPIE uses an iterative policy-judge loop: 
1. A policy agent proposes and refines prompts. 
2. A judge agent evaluates the prompt and generated image. 
3. Global-relative feedback preserves the most harmful directions found so far while tracking progress. 
4. Cumulative Adversarial Decoding turns accumulated feedback into token-level guidance, helping exploration while preserving prompt diversity and implicitness. 

Across standard and safety-aligned text-to-image models, as well as a commercial API, AdvPIE outperformed existing red-teaming baselines. In a post-acceptance controlled pilot against GPT‑6-Astra with the same feedback framework, matched image-query budgets, and prompt constraints, AdvPIE achieved 1.88× the automated successful red-team rounds per active minute. Implicit vulnerabilities require specialized, proactive red-teaming systems. A framework built for this task can find safety failures substantially faster. 

As frontier AI becomes more capable, safety cannot rely only on known attacks and static guardrails. We need tools that 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐲𝐞𝐭 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫.

text:
We turned Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Pi, @opencode and other coding harnesses into RL environments. No changes to the harnesses, no changes to the training code. Any open model, any task set, fully open source my friends!

Same model, same weights: 62% under Mini-SWE-Agent, 33% under Claude Code. But training inside a real harness normally means reimplementing it as an environment, so most models get trained in a scaffold nobody actually ships.

The fix is a proxy, not a rewrite. The harness thinks it's talking to a model API. It's actually talking to a capture proxy that speaks the 4 formats coding agents use (OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages, Gemini), forwards to @vllm_project, records the exact token IDs and logprobs vLLM sampled, and hands TRL sequences it can train on. The harness becomes the environment. 10 harnesses run through it today, none modified.

And because you control the reward, you can shape behavior the harness never asked for. We added a small bonus for solving a task in fewer tool calls: on tasks it already solved, the model now uses 31% fewer calls, in every harness, and about half under Codex.

Tested on LFM2.5-2.6B from @liquidai:
→ Train in one harness: better mostly in that harness (OpenCode 34% → 58%).
→ Train in 4 at once: better in all 4 (42% → 54%).
→ SFT on 3,189 rollouts from Qwen3.8-27B instead: plateaus at 47.5%, below both RL runs.

Everything is open and reproducible: the capture proxy in OpenEnv, the trainer in TRL, the tasks, the SFT data, the training code and all 7 trained models. Bigger models and bigger runs next.

Full guide: https://t.co/sKZURuOcza

text: Good summary of the currently deployed privacy functionality on Zcash vs Monero
author: zooko
quoted_text:
For everyone who keeps asking why I am adding @Zcash but not @monero to my Tools directory - here is my response.

For hiding which earlier coins a transaction spends, I prefer Ironwood's design to Monero's current ring signatures. I am comparing Monero as it runs today with a fully shielded transfer that stays inside Zcash's Ironwood pool.

Monero hides each input among 16 ring members: the real output being spent and 15 other outputs used as decoys. The ages of those decoys need to resemble actual spending patterns. OSPEAD research (funded by the Monero community) found a mismatch between the two distributions.

Its preliminary estimate is that an adversary's best guess is right about 23.5% of the time on average, roughly 1 in 4.2, rather than the 6.25% of random guessing. The observer usually cannot confirm which guesses were right, and the best guess is still wrong most of the time. But the estimated hit rate is nearly 4 times random guessing.

Ironwood works differently. A spend proves the coin exists somewhere in the Ironwood pool, that the spender holds its key, and that the amounts add up, all without revealing which coin it was. The proof uses Halo 2, which needs no trusted setup. Each spend also publishes a nullifier, a unique tag that stops double spending without pointing back to the coin.

That leaves no list of candidates for decoy age analysis to rank. Some things are still visible, including fees, timing, and technical details like action counts, so wallet behavior and network privacy still matter. And proving a coin is somewhere in the pool does not make every coin in the pool an equally likely match.

Monero is developing FCMP++ to replace its rings of 16 with membership proofs covering eligible outputs across the chain, described by its developers as more than 150 million outputs. Zcash's shielded pools already prove membership across the whole pool, although FCMP++ is a different protocol with a different membership set. FCMP++ remains in beta stressnet (not active on Monero mainnet yet).

My recommendation specifically concerns fully shielded transfers that stay within one pool. For hiding which coins are spent under those conditions, Ironwood is the design I prefer today. FCMP++ will warrant a fresh comparison when it is deployed.

Corrections welcome from both sides.

text:
credits is an artwork about belief

each credit was created from a private payment - an $8 transaction on x money

each transaction id, originally visible only to sender and recipient, was converted to a sha-256 hash to create an artwork made of four 8x8 printing plates in cmyk (cyan, magenta, yellow and black)

the transaction id and settlement timestamp became public source data for the onchain artwork

the x money transaction settlement time (in seconds) determined which plates print - there are 15 different possible combinations of cmyk, so this process repeats 4 x per minute

if the original transaction id contained an 8, the resulting artwork metadata keeps track of each

the rarity calculation considers the color combination, the number of active pixels, the space they occupy after the plates shift, the number of 8s in the transaction id, and the registration of the plates

these qualities are measured against the completed collection and translated into a credit rating between 80 and 800

the rating measures those traits - it cannot account for every reason someone might value an image

the rating is fixed - the price is whatever someone is willing to pay

80 credits can be burned to create a statement

the collector chooses which credits to use and how to arrange them - their individual ratings are added together, and their colors become the material of the new artwork

a statement can take different visual forms without changing its rating

statements can also be overprinted - one is burned into another, combining their ink, ratings and histories

balance is the proposed next form

under this design, a statement can be permanently surrendered for its rating in divisible erc-20 tokens - one point becomes one balance

the statement is locked rather than destroyed - its artwork and history remain, but it can no longer be transferred

its quantity and color composition can move independently

each receiving wallet gets one non-transferable erc-721 artwork

the artwork stays with the wallet and reads its current balance of the transferable erc-20 token

the tokens move - the artwork updates

if the wallet holds nothing, the artwork remains and displays zero

when balances meet, their colors mix in proportion to the amounts received - when they split, each part carries a share of that mixture

the colors preserve an aggregate ancestry, not a traceable list of individual credits or statements

exchange custody can mix them further - a buyer may receive the exchange’s mixture rather than the particular colors a seller deposited

someone who never owned a credit or a statement can inherit their colors

credits, statements and balances can exist at the same time

some people keep the individual marks, some compose them into pages, and some surrender the page for something they can divide and exchange

others may simply prefer the balance artwork

composition reduces the number of surviving credits, overprinting reduces the number of surviving statements, and surrender moves statements out of circulation while releasing their accumulated rating as balance

the appetite for liquidity becomes one of the forces shaping all three collections

but making something divisible does not mean someone will want to buy it - actual liquidity still requires buyers and funded markets

balance offers divisibility, not a promise of demand

the market becomes a medium - its activity changes the distribution of the work, and when trading stops, that distribution remains

the price can disappear, the artwork cannot

text:
People assume that in an AI doing formal verification world, they can take their existing codebase, ask AI to prove it correct, and get either a proof or a bug.

Sadly reality has a few bones to pick with this, and one of them is the "existing codebase" part. And that's due to the good ol' halting problem.

The short of it is that there is no general purpose algorithm that takes any program and input and correctly determines whether it will terminate or run forever. With a few mathematical flourishes we can extend that to "Rice's theorem" and prove this is true for any nontrivial semantic property, meaning we can't automatically prove arbitrary things about arbitrary programs.

Now obviously we can prove some things about some programs, or else formal verification wouldn't exist as a field. The trick is that we write the code in a style suitable for verification. One example of this is totality: in Lean, all functions must be guaranteed to return a value for all inputs. If we want some code that runs forever (like f.ex a server), instead of `while true` we do `while (i < 10^60)` so that it's guaranteed to terminate and return a value (after the end of the universe).

(Totality is also why, in Lean, `1/0 == 0`. If you convert your code to Lean without accounting for this, you could have correct lean but incorrect code!)

Another "style" we use is state machines. Even if your code doesn't quite fit an SM architecture, if you want to prove it at scale, you're probably going to go with a state machine. State machines are the carcinisation of provable code.

Hopefully by now the problem is clearer: even if your codebase is objectively correct, it might not be in the right shape to be proven correct!

Okay, just have the AI rewrite your codebase into another form, right? Two problems. One: you don't know if you've introduced errors in the rewrite because you can't prove them equivalent (since one of them is not in a provable shape). Two: making code more verifiable can make it worse on other metrics, like modifiability, performance, and complexity. And now you've got the old bugbear of software engineers, the dreaded tradeoff.

Now, don't get me wrong, formal verification has a huge role in the future of software, but it's not going to be a breezy "prove my Ruby thx" Claude prompt. It's still going to take work and expertise on our parts to prove our code, and to strike the right balance between formal verification and other forms of correctness.

This is one reason I'm so excited to be working at @AntithesisHQ , which tackles a lot of the same properties as proof methods, but verifies them with "deterministic simulation testing" and fuzzing instead of with a proofs. So it's not as thorough and doesn't give you confidence in all inputs, but it automatically works on pretty much any code shape. I've literally grabbed open source projects off Github, told Claude "check properties XYZ in Antithesis thx", and gotten bug reports back. No state machine rewrites needed.

On August 6, 2025, a Manhattan jury found me guilty of one count: conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business under 18 U.S.C. § 1960. They hung on money laundering and sanctions. I have not been sentenced. A motion for acquittal is still pending. Retrial of the hung counts is set for April 26, 2027.

Fifteen days later, on August 21, Acting Assistant Attorney General Matthew Galeotti, head of the Justice Department's Criminal Division, said this in a published speech:

"Our view is that merely writing code, without ill-intent, is not a crime."

And: "where the evidence shows that software is truly decentralized and solely automates peer-to-peer transactions, and where a third party does not have custody and control over user assets, new 1960(b)(1)(C) charges against the third-party will not be approved."

"Generally, developers of neutral tools, with no criminal intent, should not be held responsible for someone else's misuse of those tools. If a third-party's misuse violates criminal law, that third-party should be prosecuted — not the well-intentioned developer."

Section 1960 is the statute I was convicted under.

I am not asking anyone to take my word for it. Read the Department's own remarks, then read what happened in my case.

quoted_text:
TLDR of @papertrade_xyz: 

nothing like this exists in a crypto; it is truly a brand new primitive

it is modeled after "bucket shops" that were popular in the early 1900s. They were gambling dens were you could wager on stock price movements without actually buying or selling the underlying. The house would always take the exact other side of your bet

This is exactly how papertrade operates. When you place a trade, the house (aka papertrade LP) takes the otherside of your trade. There is no orderbook; the trade is exactly executed at the HL oracle mid price

Now where does the LP funds from?
Incredibly, the LP starts at 0 - no one prefunds it. The LP counts on the skill of the average trader being poor and thus in aggregate a losing position. A fee is skimmed off the top of winning trades (none from losing) to also skew the LP positive

What if the LP doesn't have sufficient funds?
Then traders owed $ are placed into a queue where they're paid out in FIFO order. Traders have to lose to payout traders who won.

$Paper Tokenomics 🧻:
Here is the very cool part - you can only earn their token by losing trades. And the emissions increase when the LP has < $2M, to encourage people to lose to backstop a dwindling LP

And then staking paper earns you the fees and profits that the papertrade LP earns.

Incredibly interesting experiment built by @izebel_eth. Best of luck on the launch! A ton of eyes on this and a lot of people who want to farm $PAPER
