text:
JUST IN: CFTC Chairman Michael Selig published a new op-ed sharing that the agency is moving ahead with a proposal for its own frameworks for crypto markets, despite the Clarity Act failing to advance.

The CFTC is proposing two new rulemaking frameworks: 

1) Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX)
2) Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM)

The big takeaway: Selig says CFTC-registered exchanges would have a federal path to offer trading in crypto assets under rules designed specifically for crypto, rather than forcing exchanges into the legacy securities frameworks.

Those federally regulated venues could also allow retail customers to trade on a margined, leveraged or financed basis. This is something state-licensed crypto exchanges cannot currently offer under the framework, Selig explained.

It’s also important to note, Selig isn’t saying every crypto asset must move onto a CFTC-registered platform since the agency doesn’t have that authority without Congress.

His argument is essentially that the U.S. waited too long for legislation, so regulators are using the authority they already have to start filling the gaps and this is one of the first steps it’s taking to do that. 

“Today’s action is just the beginning. The CFTC is starting the process of addressing gaps in crypto-asset market structure and creating clear rules of the road for innovators and market participants,” Selig said. 

“We haven’t solved every problem, nor can agency action substitute indefinitely for a statutory framework passed by Congress, but we must do what we can.”

text:
Sixth question on AI.
Does AI need to be a zero-sum race between the US and China?
Many influential voices in tech as well as the current administration argue that it does. (See, for example, https://t.co/63jNKZIGON, https://t.co/82WRjDEklx, https://t.co/3isNlCWI2U and this from the White House, https://t.co/roDrwiWjIj).

There are many aspects of these arguments, but I would like to focus on three that have received less attention than they deserve.

The first aspect is that this framing typically assumes that there is a single direction of progress for AI, and the US and China are racing along this dimension toward superintelligence or at the very least some sort of powerful AI that will confer huge military and strategic advantages to the winner. If, on the other hand, the US and China are developing these technologies in different directions, there is much more room for coordination and even for each country learning from the other’s best practices.

My reading of the evidence is that there are huge differences in the American and Chinese approaches. The US is focused on foundation models, such as frontier large language models. China is also investing – and arguably catching up – in these models, but there is much greater emphasis in China on applications of AI (with the government setting targets for the spread of AI across industries, https://t.co/1yimDjGmzK).

This reflects several factors, in my assessment. First, Chinese AI investments started with government demands for surveillance technologies and government-supplied data to AI companies (e.g., https://t.co/GXWDWukQty). Second, China is facing a huge demographic transformation, which will create scarcity of labor in the near future. This encourages companies to integrate robotics and AI much more actively into the production process (and China accounts for 59% of all robot installations in the world, https://t.co/YQjXLWZwrs). Third, applications and integration of these technologies into the production process requires a lot of engineering. China has a large and very well-trained supply of engineers (whereas the US has far fewer engineers and a lot of engineering talent is currently going to Silicon Valley, which hasn’t focused on applications). Fourth, China was relatively late in catching the “artificial general intelligence,” AGI, bug, although now there is more emphasis on this in China as well.

Whatever the exact causes, this difference in approach implies that there is plenty for the US to learn from China as well as the other way around.

The second aspect is that the zero-sum framing ignores or downplays the crucial need for global coordination. This framing claims that the strategic and military advantage that powerful AI will create is all that matters. But the race to AGI also poses huge risks (and this is true regardless of whether this race is truly advancing toward superintelligence or just producing distorted intelligence, as I argued in my first post in this series). And these risks are global. If the US and China are racing toward AGI with no guardrails and coordination, even the follower (probably China) will have models capable of creating havoc. In this case, racing without any global coordination is a recipe for disaster.
The third aspect of the problem is that this framing narrows the scope for any kind of coordination on other global issues between the US and China – including climate change, pandemics, nuclear nonproliferation and world peace. Tellingly, climate cooperation between the US and China has now largely stalled).

Let me add that I’m saying all of this not as an admirer of the Chinese system. On the contrary, I have been a vocal critic of both the Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese development strategy since Why Nations Fail (https://t.co/NMlp4VprG7) and I have argued that the Chinese success has some of its roots in severe labor repression (https://t.co/14SDaw2Y8H).

Indeed, this argument does not ignore the fact that China has an authoritarian, repressive regime, and it is using AI for surveillance and to stamp out dissent. Global coordination and efforts to set up reasonable rules that apply to all parties do not require the counterparty to be fully democratic or ruled by angels. In fact, sometimes it is more important to set up such a global framework when dealing with dangerous adversaries (as the arms-control treaties that the US and the Soviets signed demonstrate).

In sum, my assessment is that it is a colossal mistake to frame the AI race as a zero-sum one between the US and China. It poisons the much-needed dialogue and coordination between the US and China on broader issues; it makes the AI race more reckless; and it discourages the building of reasonable guardrails and regulations.

The last point is particularly relevant, and makes me sometimes say: if China did not exist, Silicon Valley would have to invent it.

a16z's Olivia Moore thinks AI's subscription-heavy monetization is an unnatural inversion of the consumer internet, and other models like ads need to come back:

"Substantially all of the consumer AI revenue thus far has come from direct subscriptions. On our web list, 85% monetize via subscriptions, another 62% via credits or extra usage payments."

"Only 13% had ads or other options where you are the product instead of paying for the product."

"If you look back at the history of the consumer internet, that's a pretty unnatural inversion. Almost all of the really big consumer technology companies we have now make the vast majority of their revenue from ads or transaction fees, not subscriptions."

"The truth is... most people don't have the funds, or don't want to spend their funds, on software."

"If you look at the top 20 consumer subscription products globally, ChatGPT is already on there, which is crazy in three and a half years. Almost all the others are media companies or big platforms like Amazon or Uber, where you have very frequent purchase behavior."

"So I'm a big believer: we have transcended the need for everyone to buy a subscription to AI, and we need to see these other business models come back."

text:
Sterling is a fantastic writer, and I appreciate him sharing the challenges of being a "befuddling" medical case 

The modern medical system is incredible right up until there's no easy answer.

Gunshot wound to the chest? You're probably surviving that. 

Terrible car accident? We're helicoptering you to the hospital, giving you a blood transfusions on the way. 

But unexplained chronic pain? Here's a pill. good luck

In my experience, medical practitioners struggle with the unexplainable. It's not that they don't care. They are structurally constrained: their training, liability and even compensation restricts their ability to operate outside of a very defined scope and tight time constraints. 

Widespread superintelligence is coming for the befuddling, idiosyncratic, and unexplainable health conditions. Patients are leveling up, becoming mini-researchers and citizen scientists. Doctors, nurses and scientists will be turbocharged to learn more, collaborate more efficiently, and get more patients healthy

This is already happening today. Bryan Johnson, Sid Sijbrandij, and Kate Rouch are already making the future patient-led medicine a reality.

The befuddling cases won’t stay befuddling.

quoted_text:
It's happening. My wife told her friends how I set up a @bot to handle weekly meal planning and grocery shopping, saving 2-3 hours per week. 

They lean forward. "I want that! How do I get that?"

The AI factories are pitching travel agents, but mundane convenience seems like a killer feature to usher the Instagram crowd to Muse/Bot/Dot/etc.

Most people right now "use AI" the way I use a Swiss Army knife to lift the tab on a soda can, so everything she describes next lands like "The Turn" of a magic trick.

Every Sunday, "Sylvia-bot" sends 15 meal ideas and we choose 5-7 based on the week. It knows to assign the easy meals to the nights when our family calendar shows football practice. It knows to use ingredients 2-3 times in different ways, like a chef balancing COGS and flavors. It knows the components of a successful taco night.

We had years of weekly grocery orders for training, so it knows the brands, flavors, and sizes we prefer as a family. (I wonder how long it will take others to get to this point without the archive.)

We're still working on the idea that "grape tomatoes and cherry tomatoes are interchangeable" and "don't buy berries that aren't on sale!"

In 5 minutes, we approve the plan. It does the shopping on H-E-B, double-checks the pantry assumptions (e.g. soy sauce, spices, etc.), adds the kids' usual extras, and emails a clean PDF of every recipe for the week.

At the end of each week, we log our favorite to a 'recipe book' memory for future rotations.

For now, my wife will scan the cart (another 5 minutes) and confirm tomorrow's pickup window. Soon, I expect our Tesla will do the grocery run on its own.

text:
For everyone who keeps asking why I am adding @Zcash but not @monero to my Tools directory - here is my response.

For hiding which earlier coins a transaction spends, I prefer Ironwood's design to Monero's current ring signatures. I am comparing Monero as it runs today with a fully shielded transfer that stays inside Zcash's Ironwood pool.

Monero hides each input among 16 ring members: the real output being spent and 15 other outputs used as decoys. The ages of those decoys need to resemble actual spending patterns. OSPEAD research (funded by the Monero community) found a mismatch between the two distributions.

Its preliminary estimate is that an adversary's best guess is right about 23.5% of the time on average, roughly 1 in 4.2, rather than the 6.25% of random guessing. The observer usually cannot confirm which guesses were right, and the best guess is still wrong most of the time. But the estimated hit rate is nearly 4 times random guessing.

Ironwood works differently. A spend proves the coin exists somewhere in the Ironwood pool, that the spender holds its key, and that the amounts add up, all without revealing which coin it was. The proof uses Halo 2, which needs no trusted setup. Each spend also publishes a nullifier, a unique tag that stops double spending without pointing back to the coin.

That leaves no list of candidates for decoy age analysis to rank. Some things are still visible, including fees, timing, and technical details like action counts, so wallet behavior and network privacy still matter. And proving a coin is somewhere in the pool does not make every coin in the pool an equally likely match.

Monero is developing FCMP++ to replace its rings of 16 with membership proofs covering eligible outputs across the chain, described by its developers as more than 150 million outputs. Zcash's shielded pools already prove membership across the whole pool, although FCMP++ is a different protocol with a different membership set. FCMP++ remains in beta stressnet (not active on Monero mainnet yet).

My recommendation specifically concerns fully shielded transfers that stay within one pool. For hiding which coins are spent under those conditions, Ironwood is the design I prefer today. FCMP++ will warrant a fresh comparison when it is deployed.

Corrections welcome from both sides.

author: sarick
quoted_text:
These are genuinely nice charts, @a16z. But you skipped circular financing, so I made a quick video on it (see below 👇).

A little about me and why this is relevant. The weekend before Lehman failed, I was on the advisory team that helped issue their final CLO. I spent the whole great financial crisis (GFC) in CDOs, CLOs, and CDS. What I took away from that period of time was EVERYTHING runs through the agreements, and those agreements are all interrelated.

So when Oracle’s 5yr CDS hit a record last week, wider than 08, I decided it was time to pay attention. We know debt informs equity, and when protection gets that expensive, you really have to start asking what if?

So let's follow the money:

→ Nvidia funds OpenAI
→ OpenAI buys compute from Oracle
→ Oracle buys chips from Nvidia

But what if demand drifts to cheaper open models (a very real concern at the moment)?

• The labs would grow slower than the projections they raised the debt on
• But they’d still owe the same
• Debt Service Coverage Ratio takes a hit
• Each company’s revenue is another one’s bill, so the whole circle of participants eventually feels it

Btw, you only really see this coming with certainty by understanding the agreements and how they work together. Normally, this takes weeks with intense iteration. But you know what? The market won’t give you weeks when it really matters... The movie Margin Call had it right: be first, be smarter, or cheat.

I’d rather be the first two, never the latter. This is one reason I built DAC: so anyone can SEE and understand the risks and opportunities through scenarios embedded across agreements, before you need them, or instantly if required.

It is very important to know your options before the trade unwinds because when it unwinds... it unwinds fast!

Now, I am not saying this will happen, but it is important to know what-ifs so one can plan and be positioned to react accordingly

The bridge data changes the interpretation of Ethereum’s $1.09B USDC decline.

If users were simply moving USDC to other chains, CCTP should have been net negative on Ethereum.

Instead, it was +$208M.

The actual gap came from issuer-side activity, where burns exceeded mints by $1.36B.

That makes the latest supply drop much more about redemptions than migration.
author: Covalent_HQ
quoted_text:
$1.09B of USDC left Ethereum this week. The first guess would be that it was bridged elsewhere.

That would make sense. USDC can move between chains through Circle’s CCTP, which burns USDC on one chain and mints it on another.

But the flow data tells a different story.

CCTP actually brought $208M more USDC into Ethereum than it took out this week.

The real outflow came from the issuer side. Authorized minters burned $1.36B more USDC than they minted, with one address accounting for 79% of the burns.

So Ethereum’s biggest USDC decline in 13 weeks wasn’t a cross-chain migration story.

It was a redemption story.

text:
David Friedberg: Rising Rates Could Trigger a Banking Shock Right Before the Midterms

@friedberg:

“We've got a rate problem.

In the last 30 days or so, right, we've seen short-term rates on treasuries climb by 60 basis points.

And so this massive increase in rates is obviously going to impact people's ability to refinance their home, buy a new car, purchase things on credit, and the majority of Americans fall under that umbrella.

And I think there's also kind of an economic challenge ahead with the rate problem, and I would argue, as I always do, that the rate problem is fundamentally rooted in the federal government and the insane spending.

And if you look at the impact that this rate is gonna have on banks, there's 4295 banks that have positive equity that report FDIC, their balance sheets every month.

Based on the actual reported balance sheet of these banks, about 95 banks are going to see an impairment of more than 20% of their equity in the last 30 days or so.

And those reports start to come out on October 30th. So the thing I worry a lot about is on October 30th, we're going to kind of see all these financial reports coming out from all the banks, all the lending institutions, and there's about 95 of them that are going to say, ‘Hey, we've got more than 20% impairment charge on our equity.’

That's going to be a massive shock, and then what are the implications of that?

And that's where we're going to start to wake up to the fact that the rate problem isn't just a purchasing problem for consumers, but it may actually have a bit of a rippling effect here in the economy, starting with the financial institutions.

So they publish their next monthly reports on the September 30th ending period on October 30th, and unfortunately, it coincides right with the election cycle.”

text:
OpenAI 也给 ChatGPT 的文字加水印了

OpenAI 今天宣布，未来几周内，欧盟用户在 ChatGPT 和 Codex 里生成的文字会带上一种看不见的水印，用来满足欧盟《人工智能法案》（EU AI Act）的要求。

顺便说一下 8 月，Anthropic 已经给 Claude 加了水印，原因也是一样的。

起因是欧盟 AI 法案的透明度条款在今年 8 月 2 日生效，要求 AI 生成的内容能被机器识别。7 月欧盟出了一份配套的行为准则，Anthropic、OpenAI、Google、Meta、微软等约 190 家签了字。

两家的差别主要在范围。

OpenAI 只在欧盟给 ChatGPT 和 Codex 默认加水印，其他地区的 ChatGPT 用户不受影响。API 这边，全球开发者可以在项目或组织设置里自己打开，部分模型今天就能用，默认关闭。

Anthropic 的方案是全球统一，水印直接做在模型层面，网页版、API、Claude Code 输出的文字都带，用户关不掉。Anthropic 给的理由是，暂时没有可靠的办法按地区区分。新模型已经带上水印，旧模型会在未来几个月陆续更新。图片和文件另外用 C2PA 标准，在文件元数据里附一段加密签名的来源说明。

两家加水印的算法都差不多，大模型生成水印时，每一步都要在几个差不多合适的词里随机挑一个。水印就是把这个“随机”换成一套带密钥的规则，让选词带上一种统计规律。人读起来没有区别，检测工具拿着密钥一算，就能判断这段话大概率出自哪家的模型。OpenAI 把自己的技术叫 textGrain，Anthropic 的原理基本相同。

检测工具两家都没对公众开放。OpenAI 只接受审核通过的研究人员和专业机构申请。Anthropic 的检测接口在内测，面向监管机构、执法部门、媒体、事实核查机构、研究人员、教育机构和有合规需求的企业。普通人想贴一段文字进去自己查，目前两家都做不到。

理论上来说，你手动稍微改写或换个开源模型润色修改下，标记就会变弱。

所以两家都强调：查不出水印，不能证明是人写的。水印也说明不了人改了多少、版权归谁、内容对不对。

真是脱裤子放屁——多此一举！

text:
Have always hated the concept of considering treasuries to be “risk free”

People take it far too literally, when the realistic lens is to view it as opportunity cost

Treasuries are only risk free in the sense that you are guaranteed to receive your principal back

However, it doesn’t account for the fact that you are taking risk through: 

1. Inflation eating away at your earnings power during that time period. There have been periods of time when real rates (rate minus CPI) are negative

2. Opportunity cost of not investing in higher yielding stocks or bonds, assuming you are being compensated correctly for the risk you are taking. The younger you are, the more opportunity cost you have

If something yields below the treasury rate, it is simply more worthwhile for you to invest that money in treasuries instead

But ultimately, the math should be based on your cost of capital, rather than the risk free rate itself

A company with 8% cost of capital should only reinvest its cash flows into investments and expansions that expect to generate higher rates of returns above 8%

Simply referring to treasuries as risk free assets doesn’t account for the entire picture, and is a pretty narrow, but somewhat helpful, way to view the world

text:
Taylor Sheridan won’t write the script for “Sicario 3” (Peaky Blinder’ Stephen Knight is on the job).

The original “Sicario” was actually Sheridan’s first script ever and the backstory is great: in 2010, Sheridan was 40 and just quit acting when the “Sons of Anarchy” producers low-balled him. 

After 15 years in Hollywood, Sheridan realized he’d never be more than a B actor.

Writing seemed liked the best option because he needed money and his wife had a kid on the way.

Sheridan says the family’s money was so tight that buying the Final Draft screenwriting software basically maxxed his wife’s credit card.

He ended up pumping out the script that would become “Sicario” (2015). Unreal.

Sheridan says he had “absolutely no idea” how to write but “knew exactly what not to do” because he had worked with “so many bad scripts” as an actor.

“Tell the story I want to tell,” he said of his approach in a 2016 interview. “Be honest and it should probably work out. I write movies I want to see about things that interest me. I assume I’m not that unique and other people will like them too.”

“Sicario” became a hit, which gave him runway to make “Hell or High High Water” (2016) and “Wind River” (2017). Sheridan calls these three films his “American Frontier” trilogy.

After those films, Paramount tapped him for “Yellowstone” and kicked off his massively successful TV run.

quoted_text:
Dropping a podcast with @vikramskr, writer of Vik's Newsletter and co-host of Semi Doped, on AI agents, memory, and the hardware behind the data center buildout.

Buying more GPUs is only one piece. Getting data to them fast enough is another.

Vik explains why memory and interconnects can leave compute sitting idle, why AI data centers need more optics, and how training and inference create different hardware demands.

We also get into a question I found interesting. Do agents always need the highest possible speed, or should we be optimizing for how much useful work they get done per token?

In this conversation we discuss

- AI agents and what they actually need to run
- AI spending and the risk of overbuilding
- Training versus inference workloads
- Copper, optical interconnects, and co-packaged optics
- SRAM, DRAM, high bandwidth memory, and storage
- Useful work per token and agent context
- New inference chips and the memory bottleneck

Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

Long coding runs shouldn’t end with a marathon chat to review.

Nightshift is a GitHub plugin for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor that gives long-running coding work a durable, reviewable contract.

It helps you leave an agent with a defined shift and come back to inspect what happened by keeping the punch list, verification, decisions, and receipts on disk.

Key features:

• Persistent punch list – keeps each work item and its verification criteria explicit across a run
• Clock-out gate – rejects a premature finish when work remains unfinished
• Receipts and history – records item-level work, checks, time, and token usage where the host provides it
• Recovery support – a watchman can recover failed sessions under supported host signals
• Flexible shift modes – run a finite task list or a time-bounded objective, including ready-made work catalogs

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Link in the reply 👇

text:
What Has Changed Since Infold’s 2025 Statement? ⁉️

Looking back at this statement from Infold in 2025 feels especially striking today.

Back then, Infold spoke proudly about Love and Deepspace bringing traditional Chinese culture to players around the world. They emphasized cultural exchange, adapting localization to the cultural and linguistic context of different markets, and even described the international recognition of Chinese culture as a “shared honor of Love and Deepspace and its players.”

And that makes me wonder: what changed?

If players were important enough to be presented as part of this shared cultural success in 2025, why does communication with those same players feel so different today?

For months, players have been asking for clarity, acknowledgement and communication — and instead, they have largely been met with silence. And by now, this silence is no longer something affecting only the Global community. Chinese players are experiencing it too.

That contrast is what I find so difficult to understand.

Cultural exchange cannot really be one-sided. You cannot celebrate your players when their participation helps demonstrate your cultural and international success, but then leave those same players without meaningful communication when things become uncomfortable.

I don’t expect Infold to agree with every criticism or respond to every demand. But if its players truly matter in the way Infold itself described in 2025, then communication should matter when things are difficult too — not only when players are part of a success story.

And perhaps that is what makes this old statement feel so different today. The silence now seems to cross the very cultural boundaries Infold once spoke so proudly about bridging.

🚨 Uber 内部用来盯 AI agent 的那套安全系统 ADR，开源了，能把公司里没人报备就偷偷用上的 AI 工具揪出来。

GitHub 上 1623 star、172 个 fork，相关论文被 MLSys 2026 接收，系统本身已经在 Uber 生产环境跑着。

现在公司里的 agent 安全基本是个黑洞：谁在用 Cursor、谁装了 Claude Code、哪个客服 agent 被人用提示词绕过去了，安全团队看不见。ADR 把这件事拆成五块来做——先把没批准的 AI 工具找出来，再观测 agent 到底调了什么工具、执行了哪些动作，然后评测防御能力、检测威胁、拦住不安全的操作。

观测这块已经在生产环境里跨 macOS、Linux、Windows 采了七种以上 AI 编程工具的轨迹；检测用的是两层结构，先高召回粗筛，再对可疑会话做深一层的推理。它还带了一个 ADR-Bench，300 多个任务、134 个 MCP server，把 17 种 agent 攻击手法全覆盖了一遍。

要说清楚的是，这次开源的是 Discovery、Sensor、ADR-Bench 和 Detector 这几块，负责拦截的 Prevention 组件和离线的 Explorer 引擎没放出来。

quoted_text:
Sharing thoughts on handling Bankr token communities, as someone who is now getting tagged as a good example for devs to follow.

-- How it started --

First, congrats. You finally have eyes on your project. People are excited about your work and they want to be a part of it.

I also know it feels suspicious for random people online to say you've earned a bunch of money. Early on I was clear in my replies that the tokens were not mine - they were launched by some unknown person using my brand. I tried to shut it down.

But the attention kept coming, and it opened up some amazing opportunities.

I'm crypto native and had been thinking about making an equity-like token integrated with the product that could be used to align users and business partners. Over three days I met with three different token launchpads. The opportunity to have these meetings, and their optimistic tone, was strongly influenced by the traction of the community tokens that I was actively disavowing.

But by that third day, the community token had a lot of traction. And people from the community were genuinely adding value -- tagging me and promoting my project in constructive ways all across twitter.

So I decided to acknowledge that community token, and hold off indefinitely on making the one I was planning.

I also spent an entire day engaging with the fast growing token community. I talked explained how my product works, and asked for help on the things it needed immediately. I also clarified that product and partnerships were my key focus.

The outcome: Harassment dropped to 0, and now I have hundreds of people working to make this project succeed. My read is that the harassment came from understandable desperation and uncertainty -- holders are exposed to significant risk when they don't know if they'll be welcomed or shunned. They are excited about your work and want to help, but also they will lose their money if you don't let them. 

Resolving that uncertainty in a fair and reasonable way turns the harassment into a constructive tailwind for your project. Now the community knows if they help you, they will also benefit from the asymmetric upside of their community token.

I was really surprised by how many people showed up out of nowhere to help in meaningful ways. This is the power of economic alignment through a token. There's now hundreds of people who have exposure to the success of my project, and are trying to make it succeed.

It would normally cost a lot to get hundreds of people to try to make your work succeed -- but with the Bankr community tokens those same people also paid around $600k in trading fees, around half of which I can use however I want.

That's an insanely good deal for your project if you're able to navigate the awkward bits.

Miraculously it's also an insanely good deal for the community, since they get the upside of the community token. The return profile here is similar to venture where almost all tokens do poorly, but the ones that do well have unimaginably high returns.

-- Going forward --
I'll keep the community updated with what I'm doing for the project, and invite them to share their perspectives on key decisions. It might be hard for devs to realize this, but many members want to see how the sausage is made and get experience with the kind of decision making you are doing -- it's intrinsically exciting to be involved in discussions around a project that has a shot at being massively successful, and it's an opportunity for the community to build those skills themselves so they can later on be like the dev that they're aspiring to learn from now. This was something I loved about DAO forums and Discords back in the day. It's amazing to have grown from being a community member myself in so many DAOs, to now running an exciting project of my own.

The community has gotten to a size where I sadly can't possibly respond to everything. I'm still reading everything but not sure if that will be possible as it continues to grow.

I'm testing using Grok to summarize all the perspectives you share on key issues, and the contributions you're making across X. 

For devs, this is the kind of unfair advantage that will make your project win. And you can bootstrap this by embracing a strong token community.

text:
今天美国十年期国债收益率一度达到 5.35% 左右，创下近 24 年新高。长期利率持续走高，会增加企业和居民新借款以及旧债再融资的成本。企业发债、居民买房买车，可能都需要支付更多利息，原来已经锁定固定利率的贷款，则暂时不会受到直接影响。

可能会有小伙伴问，如果是这么坏的预期，为什么美股还在上涨，AI 投资是一个重要原因。科技企业持续建设数据中心、购买芯片和服务器，这些支出变成了相关供应商的订单和收入。比如英伟达截至今年 7 月 26 日的一个季度，数据中心收入同比增长了 117%。市场预期这部分需求还会继续增长，也就愿意为相关公司的未来盈利买单。而英伟达、微软等大型科技公司在指数中的权重较高，它们上涨，就能带动标普和纳斯达克。

除了 AI，其他行业的盈利预期也在提供支撑。FactSet 在 10 月 2 日预计，标普 500 第三季度盈利同比增长 29.5%，全部 11 个行业都预计实现增长。利率上升会给估值带来压力，但如果企业盈利增长足够快，股价仍然可能上涨。所以，融资成本上升和美股上涨可以同时发生，后续要看企业实际赚到的钱，能不能跟上市场预期。

对于 $BTC 情况就不同了。美债收益率越高，投资者放弃利息收入、选择持有 Bitcoin  就越需要对它未来的上涨空间有信心。如果现货和 ETF 持续有资金买入，可以抵消部分高利率压力；如果买盘减少、卖盘增加，价格就会承压。科技股上涨可以带动市场情绪，但 BTC 仍然需要实际买盘支撑。

author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
In 2015, Bitcoin was right there, in front of me.
I ran into it ten times. I never stopped. Like everyone else, I shrugged, and I let it go by.

The hard part was not understanding Bitcoin. 
The hard part was stopping for it. Giving it an hour, a page, one real try. The people who got it were not smarter. They had tried.

Eleven years later, I feel the exact same thing about Bittensor. A network where artificial intelligence belongs to no one, where the rules are public, and whose currency is capped like bitcoin. All around me, the same "this is too complicated for me."

This time, I stopped for it. And I wrote the book that lets you do the same in a weekend.

I wrote it for people who know nothing about any of this. Every technical word explained once, in one sentence. A city, its districts, its craftsmen and its jury to understand the machine without a single diagram. And the risks as a whole part of the book, not a footnote.

It will not tell you what to buy. It predicts nothing. It gives you what you need to judge for yourself.

"The Bitcoin of AI" is out October 12 on Amazon, in English and in French.

If someone around you says "I don't get any of this," I wrote it for them.

In 2015, nobody handed me this book.
In 2026, I am handing it to you.

You should be able to run it on a machine that never touches the internet.
You should be able to run it while your laptop is closed.
You should be able to reach it from the apps you already use.
You should be able to choose how your agent thinks.
You should be able to read the prompt it runs on.
You should be able to see every tool it has, and turn off the ones you don't want.
You should be able to teach it something once and never explain it again.
You should be able to know what it did, and when, and why.
You should be able to export your agent.
You should be able to read the code.
You should be able to change the code.
Your agent should be yours.

text:
Are prediction markets biased by white men? Republicans? Young people?

Dartmouth professor Eric Zitzewitz analyzed 145 years of election prediction market data, spanning multiple exchanges and countries. His findings:

• No systematic evidence of political bias across different eras, countries, and offices.
• No systematic evidence of pricing bias based on candidates’ race, gender, or age in the recent elections studied.
• Traders weren’t always representative of the voting population, yet that didn’t translate into systematic bias in election forecasts.

The paper points to a powerful mechanism: people who spot a mispriced outcome have a financial incentive to correct it. Even if some participants trade on personal preferences, informed traders keep prices grounded in reality.

Open competition incentivizes research, challenges consensus, and gives the best ideas a chance to surface. People are rewarded for being right, regardless of their background or preferences.

The paper does find some pricing biases, including slight overpricing of longshots and underpricing of favorites. Its central finding on election markets remains: no systematic evidence of political or demographic bias.

In an increasingly polarized world, these markets give us something valuable: an impartial source of information shaped by people with an incentive to get it right.

Reflection launches Beam today.

Recommend reading the founders 
Beautiful ode to open innovation!
author: sreeramkannan
quoted_text:
We are introducing Beam today, a 500b open model that excels in coding, agentic, and scientific workloads.

Beam is very token-efficient, pre-trained from scratch, and scaled with the largest RL run documented openly we are aware of.

Getting here was challenging, rewarding, and personal.

I immigrated to the USA during childhood when my parents got jobs as scientists at PNNL, a national lab located in a rural town in Washington state.

Growing up, I developed an interest in physics because it was grounded in simple principles, was foundational, and had long-term impact.

Physics was the foundational science of the 20th century. The first general computer (ENIAC), the transistor, GPS, and much of modern technology had its roots in physics.

In 2016, during my graduate studies, I noticed the birth of a new foundational science - Artificial Intelligence.

AlphaGo, the superintelligent Go agent developed by DeepMind, had come out and made me feel what was about to come.

A neural network, trained to imitate human players, and then improve itself through trial and error, mastered the most intellectually challenging board game in the world.

What surprised me about AlphaGo is how it was conceptually simple, general, and scalable. The system could in principle improve itself forever, it was just a function of compute.

This is when I became “AGI pilled” as they say.

I switched from physics to AI because I thought this would become the root node science of the 21st century, much like physics was the root node science of the 20th century.

I believe that working on foundational science is not enough on its own. Foundational science must also remain open and widely accessible.

We remember Newton for his contributions to physics, but he was also an alchemist.

Alchemy was done in secret, because the artificial production of gold was deemed lucrative but also dangerous with the potential do destroy entire economies. Newton even wrote his alchemy notebooks in cypher.

On the other hand, Principia was published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, the knowledge was made widely available, passed down for generations in what we now call Newton’s laws.

The computer, transistor, GPS were possible to build because physics as a science was open. Openness creates an ecosystem of innovation.

The notion of openness, which is a core tenet of scientific discovery, has also become a guiding principle for how foundational technology gets built and distributed.

The internet was built on open protocols. The most widely used operating systems are open. The field of cybersecurity exists because strong encryption protocols were made open in the 1990s.

Open also means safer. The best defence is a distributed one. Commonly used open source software is robust and battle-tested because it is inspected and patched by a community of developers.

AI is different but also similar to software in many ways, though with a much larger surface area of vulnerabilities. It is impossible for a small group of safety researchers working in secrecy to remediate all of the potential issues regardless of their intentions. It is like entrusting a handful of white blood cells to protect your body.

AI is both foundational as a science and a technology, and the safest way that also ensures the benefits of AI are distributed evenly is by making it open.

I’m excited for what developers and scientists build and learn from this model, and for Beam to play a small part in ensuring that AI is made widely accessible, safe, and beneficial to all.

I was early to both. I bought and sold SWORDCAT, and I bought KNIGHTCAT and still hold. I genuinely love the meme. I think it’s generational.

When KNIGHTCAT launched, I saw the CA in the IG bio, researched the creator, and found the connection to Higgsfield. Higgsfield ambassador confirmed the relationship, and the Knightcat name was already being used by Sickmainai.

I hate PVP but there’s one thing I hate more and that’s THEFT

My argument isn’t that creating the original content automatically gives someone legal ownership of every token using the meme.

It’s that if you create the character, artwork and content that a token is built around, you should benefit from the value your work creates.

SWORDCAT should have approached the original creator from the beginning if they wanted to build around that content. Instead, the content was taken directly from their page.

That’s what created this entire PVP situation.

Then Beeple, who hasn’t posted about a meme token in ages, posts the SWORDCAT ticker and gives it another massive momentum boost.

My opinion:

If KNIGHTCAT stays committed to delivering original content, I think it ultimately flips SWORDCAT

Not because of PVP, but because KNIGHTCAT has the original creator behind it

At this point, I don’t see the reason to attack KNIGHTCAT or the creator. Everyone who bought SWORDCAT before today has had the opportunity to take profit, and I actually like how things worked out for those holders.

If KNIGHTCAT keeps executing, I believe this ultimately ends with the original creators and KNIGHTCAT holders on top

text:
i have some perspective here since i got onboarded at 17 and have decided to stick with it

1. it’s on the verge of embarrassing to publicly endorse the industry, let alone work in it. requires you to be dead to shame and not care about what your peers think of you. asking a current 18-22 year old to leave the panopticon of social media and the constant stare of linkedin is the career equivalent of asking someone to walk on all fours in public. 

2. the long term useful parts (payments/tokenization/credit/perps kinda) are extremely low visibility and lack the perceived exponential growth prospects of ai. most of the very interesting work is hidden behind financial infrastructure firms that are abstracted away from anyone’s general knowledge about markets. the other issue is that the long term useful parts are very gated and/or lean teams that aren’t really seeking to develop new talent.

3. gambling is the only thing that will pay you comparably to ai/hft. why in the world would a talented young person decide to go grind in payments when a perps app will pay you triple cash + an enormous sum in token comp? even with an offer from said perps app, why not go trade equity options at some t2 hft firm when first year tc is half a mil AND mom is still proud of you? do not underestimate gen z’s chronic short termism and preference for wealth and status now.

now just to be clear, these are not entirely bad problems. this industry is currently in a darwinian evolution stage, thinning out the herd of idiots and scammers for an intelligent and cunning breed of financial engineers. a lot of other smart young people i’ve met who are sticking it out have really high intuition on markets.

if you are an industry leader/investor and care about your legacy, take some time to find and culture young talent. all of the greatest financial minds live on through their protégés compounding their philosophy over generations of new companies and employees. become a person whose values spawn great companies, funds, and people long after your time.

quoted_text:
Instinct in group chats

Starting today, early access users can add Instinct to group chats. A new Instinct joins and works for the whole group.

Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread. Your friends don't even need Instinct to join in.

A few things it’s good at:
- Planning a weekend trip with friends, including dates and arrival times
- Coordinating logistics with a roommate
- Getting tickets as soon as they go on sale, then splitting the cost and sending one to everyone
- Running a fantasy league, keeping standings, settling rules disputes, and reminding everyone to set their lineups
- Sorting out carpool schedules - works out who’s driving each day from everyone’s schedules
- Organizing Thanksgiving, keeping track of who’s bringing what and ordering the shopping list

Group chats are new territory for Instinct, and we put a lot of care into getting the permissions right. Here’s how it works:
- Your personal Instinct asks before connecting with the group’s Instinct. You choose which groups to trust and can remove trust at any time.
- The group’s Instinct has no direct access to your personal accounts. Your Instinct checks your permissions before sharing information or taking action.
- If someone new joins the group, all pending replies from your Instinct are held until you grant it permission to share with the expanded group.

Group chats are available to all of our early access users, and will be rolling out to everyone soon. To join early access for this release, ask your Instinct to put you on the list.

quoted_text:
I’m spending $2.6 million on female health…

Here are 5 facts most women don’t know

#1
Your labia minora folds can fuse together after menopause.

When estrogen declines, vaginal tissue tends to thin and dry out… it’s rare, but this can lead to fusing.

More commonly, this hormonal decline can affect lubrication, urinary function, and/or sex. Many women don’t realize these conditions are treatable.

#2
Your voice may change every month…

The vocal folds have receptors for sex hormones, and estrogen and progesterone levels are constantly rising or falling

Researchers have measured differences in pitch, voice quality, vocal cord movement, etc. across the menstrual cycle

It’s debated because not all studies agree on the size or direction of these changes

#3
Women metabolize some drugs differently…

For example, Ambien.

Studies found that women had around 45% higher blood concentrations of ambien (zolpidem) than men after the same dose. Women also cleared the drug from the bloodstream more slowly.

In 2013, the FDA cut the recommended starting dose for women in half.

#4
Your brain changes during pregnancy…

And some parts shrink

The extreme hormonal changes are linked to the brain remodeling itself. Gray matter volume and cortical thickness both decrease

In a 2016 human study, changes occurred in regions involved in social cognition.

#5
A lot of female anatomy is named after men.

It was common to name body parts after a person associated with describing or studying it.

So we ended up with…

Fallopian tubes --> Gabriele Falloppio
Bartholin’s glands --> Caspar Bartholin the Younger
Skene’s glands --> Alexander Johnston Chalmers Skene
Gartner’s ducts --> Hermann Treschow Gartner
Müllerian ducts --> Johannes Peter Müller

--

Female health is severely understudied… this is why I am becoming the world’s most measured woman.

I’m gathering 14 million data points on my menstrual cycle and collecting 1,900 biomarkers across skin, brain, microbiome, smell, taste, etc.

I’ll be sharing all the results here

> About $50M of inflows in the first three days, over $10M a day, with $10 to 20M in daily volume. Some assets with larger market caps got ETFs this year and saw less of both.

> This was not a reaction to the price. Bitwise published institutional research on NEAR over a year ago, launched a European ETP, became one of the largest validators on the network, and runs an MPC node for chain signatures. The ETF came after all of that.

> The CoinMarketCap era is over. Mainstream investors do not rank assets by their position on a list. His pitch for NEAR is one sentence: a co-inventor of the LLM built a blockchain where people and AI agents use models and move assets across chains, and it is growing fast. No crypto PhD required.

> The theme of 2026 is that investors are comfortable with Bitcoin and are looking at what else they want exposure to. NEAR is a first class candidate for that.

> Investors have matured past page views. In the early internet people counted eyeballs; twenty years later they count revenue per user and retention. Crypto is at the same point, and NEAR has the things that get counted now: usage, revenue, and buybacks tied to it.

> Against AI platforms with traction, NEAR at around $5B is roughly a tenth of the average valuation. His words: it might be the cheapest thing you have ever seen.

> The ETF stakes on behalf of the holder. One less decision the investor has to get right.

> Nobody buys a Bitwise ETF for exposure to Bitwise. They buy it because they have conviction in NEAR.

You should be able to use smarter models in your agent.
You should be able to use cheaper models in your agent.
You should be able to use local models in your agent.
You should be able to use a different model for every job.
You should be able to switch models in the middle of a conversation.
You should be able to choose what data your agent has.
You should be able to choose what it remembers and what it forgets.
You should be able to choose what computer your agent runs on.
You should be able to run it on a machine that never touches the internet.
You should be able to run it while your laptop is closed.
You should be able to reach it from the apps you already use.
You should be able to choose how your agent thinks.
You should be able to read the prompt it runs on.
You should be able to see every tool it has, and turn off the ones you don't want.
You should be able to teach it something once and never explain it again.
You should be able to know what it did, and when, and why.
You should be able to export your agent.
You should be able to read the code.
You should be able to change the code.
Your agent should be yours.

text:
THORChain cofounder Chad Barraford admits 4 operators could halt THORChain, but argues Bitcoin and Ethereum can be stopped by even fewer

Laura: You said, quote, 'A chain may claim to have hundreds of validators, but that number means very little if most of them are operated by the same entities, hosted in the same data centers, or selected through a closed process.'"

"But THORChain itself has less than hundreds. And as we mentioned earlier, there are just 4 operator addresses that control 39 nodes. So do you think that THORChain passes your own litmus test?"

Chad: "Yeah. I think when it comes to evaluating how decentralized a protocol is, number of validators, not a good way to do it. And I'm not citing THORChain as decentralized because there's 115-ish validators. I'm saying it's decentralized because it has 50, 60, whatever the number is, individual operators across the world, which is better than Bitcoin, right?"

"Bitcoin's got 3, like, mining pools together would be 51% of the computing. Same thing for Ethereum. They've got, like, what, 3 or 4 operators with the major validators of Ethereum, and you would have the same situation. And most of those are, by the way, corporate entities, like Coinbase and Binance and these kinds of things."

"THORChain is more decentralized than Bitcoin and Ethereum, by the definition that you're granting to me in this moment."

"If you look at, like, halting, meaning the ability to stop the production of blocks, you would need 1/3 plus 1. It's something different if you categorize it as, like, a 2/3 majority to control the blockchain rather than stopping it."

"Even if you take the lesser of the two and you do, like, 1/3 plus 1, you can get 4 operators to, you know, stop the entire protocol. I don't know why they would do that, because you'd be burning your own RUNE to zero, which is not really in their financial interest to do so. But theoretically, on paper, they could do that."

"There's only, like, 3 entities you would need for Bitcoin, and, like, 1 or 2, or whatever the number is, for Ethereum. That's just, like, that is the world, right?"

text:
Despite coming to Colosseum with little (professional) investing experience, @mrinko taught me so much about what true conviction looks like, and how to take your non-consensus beliefs and make them a reality.

He's been such an asset to our team, I can't really fit it all into a tweet. We'll miss having him of course, but thankfully he's not going too far. 

I can't think of a better place for him than MetaDAO, and I'm excited to see what he does in this next chapter.
author: sacha
quoted_text:
Some personal news: I recently joined MetaDAO.

Working at Colosseum with Matty, Clay, Nate, and Max was a dream job. I learned a tremendous amount from each of them, and I will miss the team deeply.

Colosseum represents the very best of our industry -- running the world’s largest hackathons, writing checks before ideas are fully formed, and building open-source tools so a thousand flowers may bloom. It’s been an honor to work with our founders, and I’m excited to keep supporting them from my new seat.

Ever since I got oneshotted in 2023, I've thought about MetaDAO every single day -- with only a few notable exceptions. And along the way, I’ve tried to help. At Delphi, that meant writing slightly verbose research reports to spread the gospel. At Colosseum, it was STAMP, the Inaugural MetaDAO Owners Meeting, and [redacted].

Now, it’s time to go all in.

I love this industry and am optimistic about what we will build. But we haven’t lived up to our own expectations. The blockchains work. And the stablecoins work. So where are all the generational businesses?

It’s not that crypto is useless. It’s that too often, we reward launching tokens more than building lasting companies. I believe MetaDAO can help change that by giving founders a better way to raise money and build businesses on the internet.

Fundraising is how we will bring decision markets to the world. Our ambition goes beyond helping founders raise money -- it’s to change how companies are run and, ultimately, how institutions and perhaps even AIs make decisions.

For three years, I’ve believed in what MetaDAO could become. Now I get to help build it alongside Prophet, Kollan, and the rest of the team.

Long live the Meta DAO

text:
[continued]

I say "almost" because there is going to be one way to maintain secrecy. Software as a service with the executable hiding behind a network connection to the cloud. But as of now, we must assume that anything shipped as an executable, or even a firmware image, is as transparent as glass. It won't keep its secrets for any longer than it takes for somebody to be motivated to throw an LLM at it.

I did not see this coming. When I wrote down the theory of open source, 30 years ago now, I thought closed source would be gradually driven towards extinction by cost gradients, but survive indefinitely in certain niches. I did not foresee it being wiped out in a technoapocalypse.

Ironically, I thought one of the application areas in which closed source would persist longest was games.

There are still some obstacles. In US law, decompilation of a binary is a derivative work of the binary that falls under whatever copyright it had. However, it is also settled law that if you decompile binary code to a precise specification of what it does, then generate fresh code from that without looking at the decompiled stuff, you're in the clear. This was the case law that allowed PC clones to exist, after Phoenix Technologies reverse engineered the original IBM PC BIOS.

The two-step process - binary to specification to unencumbered code - will no longer takes a large number of programmers and years of development time. With an LLM, it's now a thing you can do in a day. Ubiquity will make it impractical to prosecute all the people who might skip the specification step.

Source code can also be covered by patents. You can be able to see their source code for a patented technique and not be able to use it without violating the law. Linux has evolved practices for dealing with this problem - one is not shipping patented video codecs, but requiring you to download them as plugins from jurisdictions where U.S. patents can't be enforced. This presents patent holders with the impractical challenge of individually suing millions of end users, assuming it can even figure out who they are. To date, AFAIK, this has not been attempted.

And that's about it. If there are any other ways left to retain software secrecy and lock-in than SaaS or patents, I can't think of any. Well, you could epoxy-pot a firmware ROM, I suppose, but that can be defeated with a heat gun and a dental pick. Device manufacturers will learn not to pay for an assembly step that has become useless. 

Forced migration from shipped binaries to tied cloud services will be tried - Adobe pioneered this, and Microsoft is pushing it as hard as they can given that their OS is a binary that has to run locally. Both companies are seeing massive user revolts over this. There is good reason to doubt that it's a strategy that can hold customers in the long term.

Also, a lot of things can't safely be tied to the cloud at all, because they can't tolerate a random network outage. Machine tools, medical devices...

A whole lot of proprietary software business models are going to collapse. Hard. One that I think might survive is tax software; being able to decompile it doesn't necessarily do you a lot of good because its actual value is tracking a ruleset that changes over time and has to be maintained by vendor specialists. But cases like this are unusual. 

I think some dirty laundry is going to get aired, too. It has long been rumored that the reason graphics card manufacturers are so stubborn in their secrecy is that they've all been committing massive intellectual-property theft on each other for decades. If this is true, it will be exposed, and the lawsuits will be entertaining.

We're entering a new world, with a lot of ancient comfortable assumptions being blown up. It's going to be fun to watch. 

2/2

text:
Derive traded $7.45B in options notional in Q3, more than the entirety of 2025.

According to @AleaResearch's latest report on @DeriveXYZ, volume grew 89.6% QoQ while the number of trades increased just 6.2%. Average trade size jumped from $47K to $84K, meaning that larger positions are driving the growth.

A few numbers worth highlighting:

• 90.4% of all onchain options premium went through Derive, its sixth consecutive quarter of market share gains.

• ETH options notional grew 243.9% to $2.57B, while ETH’s share of premium matched BTC’s at 34.2%.

• Quarterly protocol fees reached $1.35M, up 35.7% QoQ.

• Options generated 67.3% of fees, up from 53.9% in Q2.

However, volume growth isn't translating proportionally into fees. Options fees rose 69.5%, while fees per dollar of options notional fell from 1.36 to 1.22 basis points.

For $DRV, 35% of protocol fees currently fund buybacks. Derive bought 2.57M DRV in Q3, roughly twice the 1.3M DRV distributed through staking emissions. Those purchases go to the DAO treasury.

The next opportunity is expanding beyond its dominant onchain position. Derive holds just 3.1% of the combined options open interest reported by Deribit, OKX, Bybit, Binance and Derive.

With holders approving V3’s move to Ethereum, the question is how much of that larger market Derive can capture, and how effectively it converts that growth into fees.

text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one

When we launched our forecast in May, VoteHub pioneered the use of prediction markets as an input in traditional election forecasting.

There’s already ample evidence that prediction markets are generally well-calibrated. Now a new NBER paper analyzing 145 years of election markets adds another piece, finding no systematic political or demographic bias in market pricing, even when traders themselves aren’t representative of the electorate.

That finding further reinforces the usefulness of Kalshi as an input alongside polling, fundamentals, and expert ratings.
author: benwfreeman1
quoted_text:
Are prediction markets biased by white men? Republicans? Young people?

Dartmouth professor Eric Zitzewitz analyzed 145 years of election prediction market data, spanning multiple exchanges and countries. His findings:

• No systematic evidence of political bias across different eras, countries, and offices.
• No systematic evidence of pricing bias based on candidates’ race, gender, or age in the recent elections studied.
• Traders weren’t always representative of the voting population, yet that didn’t translate into systematic bias in election forecasts.

The paper points to a powerful mechanism: people who spot a mispriced outcome have a financial incentive to correct it. Even if some participants trade on personal preferences, informed traders keep prices grounded in reality.

Open competition incentivizes research, challenges consensus, and gives the best ideas a chance to surface. People are rewarded for being right, regardless of their background or preferences.

The paper does find some pricing biases, including slight overpricing of longshots and underpricing of favorites. Its central finding on election markets remains: no systematic evidence of political or demographic bias.

In an increasingly polarized world, these markets give us something valuable: an impartial source of information shaped by people with an incentive to get it right.

text:
Meta、微软收紧员工内部使用 Claude

据 The Information 10 月 5 日报道，Meta 和微软都在减少员工内部使用 Anthropic 的 Claude，转向自家模型和工具。

Meta 这边，内部数据显示，使用 Claude Code 的员工从年初约 6 万人降到最近约 3 万人。一部分原因是春季裁员，Meta 当时 7.8 万人的团队砍掉了约 10%。更大的原因是 Meta 在推自家的 Muse Spark 系列模型和编程工具：对标 Claude Code 的 Muse Code 有超过 6000 名员工在用，8 月起已开始找外部客户测试；另一款只在内部使用的 MetaCode 用户超过 3 万。

微软这边，原本预计今年内部在 Anthropic 上至少花 10 亿美元，这个数字已被砍掉三分之一以上。管理层要求员工少用 Claude，改用微软自己的工具，工程师被引导转向 GitHub Copilot 的命令行版本。

微软还整体收紧了员工的 AI 用量。云和 AI 部门有 6 万多人，此前每人每月可以在 AI 模型上花 10 万美元，最近多数情况下降到约 1 万美元。这个额度管的是所有 AI 模型，不单是 Claude。报道说，部分工程师对此有怨言，觉得不能再随意用模型了。

需要分开看的是，微软企业客户通过微软平台购买 Anthropic 服务的支出仍在增长。这次收缩的是两家公司自己员工的用量。

背景是 AI 编程工具的账单越来越大。工程师一天让 AI 写几小时代码，消耗的 Token（模型处理文本的计量单位）很容易折算成上千美元，大公司开始算账，也开始拿自研模型替代。

9 月 The Information 还报道过，Nvidia、Palantir 和 Booz Allen Hamilton 收紧了对 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 部分先进模型的使用，原因是担心模型厂商留存或学习企业内部数据。

text:
We are introducing Beam today, a 500b open model that excels in coding, agentic, and scientific workloads.

Beam is very token-efficient, pre-trained from scratch, and scaled with the largest RL run documented openly we are aware of.

Getting here was challenging, rewarding, and personal.

I immigrated to the USA during childhood when my parents got jobs as scientists at PNNL, a national lab located in a rural town in Washington state.

Growing up, I developed an interest in physics because it was grounded in simple principles, was foundational, and had long-term impact.

Physics was the foundational science of the 20th century. The first general computer (ENIAC), the transistor, GPS, and much of modern technology had its roots in physics.

In 2016, during my graduate studies, I noticed the birth of a new foundational science - Artificial Intelligence.

AlphaGo, the superintelligent Go agent developed by DeepMind, had come out and made me feel what was about to come.

A neural network, trained to imitate human players, and then improve itself through trial and error, mastered the most intellectually challenging board game in the world.

What surprised me about AlphaGo is how it was conceptually simple, general, and scalable. The system could in principle improve itself forever, it was just a function of compute.

This is when I became “AGI pilled” as they say.

I switched from physics to AI because I thought this would become the root node science of the 21st century, much like physics was the root node science of the 20th century.

I believe that working on foundational science is not enough on its own. Foundational science must also remain open and widely accessible.

We remember Newton for his contributions to physics, but he was also an alchemist.

Alchemy was done in secret, because the artificial production of gold was deemed lucrative but also dangerous with the potential do destroy entire economies. Newton even wrote his alchemy notebooks in cypher.

On the other hand, Principia was published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, the knowledge was made widely available, passed down for generations in what we now call Newton’s laws.

The computer, transistor, GPS were possible to build because physics as a science was open. Openness creates an ecosystem of innovation.

The notion of openness, which is a core tenet of scientific discovery, has also become a guiding principle for how foundational technology gets built and distributed.

The internet was built on open protocols. The most widely used operating systems are open. The field of cybersecurity exists because strong encryption protocols were made open in the 1990s.

Open also means safer. The best defence is a distributed one. Commonly used open source software is robust and battle-tested because it is inspected and patched by a community of developers.

AI is different but also similar to software in many ways, though with a much larger surface area of vulnerabilities. It is impossible for a small group of safety researchers working in secrecy to remediate all of the potential issues regardless of their intentions. It is like entrusting a handful of white blood cells to protect your body.

AI is both foundational as a science and a technology, and the safest way that also ensures the benefits of AI are distributed evenly is by making it open.

I’m excited for what developers and scientists build and learn from this model, and for Beam to play a small part in ensuring that AI is made widely accessible, safe, and beneficial to all.

text:
按照 SemiAnalysis 的测试结果：同样 200 美元，Claude 订阅的 Token 用量约为 OpenAI 的 5 倍

半导体和 AI 产业研究机构 SemiAnalysis 实测了 Anthropic、OpenAI 等九家的 AI 订阅套餐。结论是，在两家都主推的日常主力模型上，Claude 订阅折算出来的价值约为 OpenAI 的 5 倍。

订阅套餐不告诉你能用多少 Token，只给一个 0 到 100% 的进度条，分 5 小时和 7 天两个窗口。SemiAnalysis 的办法是一种 Token 一种 Token 地测：反复发请求，记下每用掉多少 Token 进度条跳一格，再按 API 标价折算成美元，得出“API 等价价值”，也就是同样的用量如果走 API 按量付费要花多少钱。测试场景是编程智能体这类重度使用。

【差距出在中档模型】

顶配模型两家差不多。200 美元套餐里，OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra 用满额度约值 2897 美元，Anthropic 的 Fable 5.1 约值 2485 美元。区别是 Claude 套餐里 Fable 最多只能占一半额度，用完这一半，另一半还能跑别的模型。

差距在中档。两家都把中档模型当日常主力推，Anthropic 是 Opus 5.5，OpenAI 是 GPT-6.1 Sol。这一档上，Claude 各套餐的价值约为 OpenAI 的 5 倍。Sol 的 API 单价比 Opus 便宜很多，按美元比对它不太公平，但 SemiAnalysis 改成直接比 Token 数量，Claude 仍然领先一大截。

OpenAI 的 Pro 套餐没有 5 小时限制，月内更容易把额度用满。SemiAnalysis 认为这一点抵不过 Opus 5.5 约 4 倍的价值差。

【OpenAI 刚砍了一半】

差距拉这么大，主要因为 OpenAI 上周刚改了套餐。9 月 29 日 DevDay 前后，OpenAI 宣布 200 美元的 Pro 档用量从 Plus 的 20 倍降到 10 倍，同时推出 500 美元的新档，独享每秒约 300 个 Token 的 Ultrafast 超快模式。老用户的旧额度保留到 10 月 29 日。

SemiAnalysis 测到的结果和官方说法一致：200 美元档每个模型的 Token 都少了一半。Sol 的折算价值跌得更多，超过 50%，因为 OpenAI 同期把 GPT-6.1 Sol 的缓存读取价格降了一半。缓存读取指多轮对话里反复发给模型的旧内容，编程智能体用量里这部分占比很大，单价一降，同样多的 Token 折算成美元就更少。新的 500 美元档，Astra 用量只比砍之前的 200 美元档多 21%。

改完之后，OpenAI 的 100、200、500 美元三档每美元换到的 Token 一样多。之前 200 美元档补贴最重，每美元价值约是 100 美元档的两倍。Anthropic 各档一直是同一个单价。

这几天 OpenAI 负责 Codex 的 Tibo 承诺，未来 28 天每天要么上线一项改进，要么给全体用户重置额度。SemiAnalysis 在文中提到，OpenAI 此前多次重置额度攒下的好感，是 Codex 最近用户猛涨的原因之一，也让 Anthropic 几次收回原定的限额收紧计划。

【两家减补贴的路子不同】

SemiAnalysis 估算，订阅只占 Anthropic 收入约一成，却吃掉超过四成的推理算力。所以两家都在减补贴。

We turned Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Pi, @opencode and other coding harnesses into RL environments. No changes to the harnesses, no changes to the training code. Any open model, any task set, fully open source my friends!

Same model, same weights: 62% under Mini-SWE-Agent, 33% under Claude Code. But training inside a real harness normally means reimplementing it as an environment, so most models get trained in a scaffold nobody actually ships.

The fix is a proxy, not a rewrite. The harness thinks it's talking to a model API. It's actually talking to a capture proxy that speaks the 4 formats coding agents use (OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages, Gemini), forwards to @vllm_project, records the exact token IDs and logprobs vLLM sampled, and hands TRL sequences it can train on. The harness becomes the environment. 10 harnesses run through it today, none modified.

And because you control the reward, you can shape behavior the harness never asked for. We added a small bonus for solving a task in fewer tool calls: on tasks it already solved, the model now uses 31% fewer calls, in every harness, and about half under Codex.

Tested on LFM2.5-2.6B from @liquidai:
→ Train in one harness: better mostly in that harness (OpenCode 34% → 58%).
→ Train in 4 at once: better in all 4 (42% → 54%).
→ SFT on 3,189 rollouts from Qwen3.8-27B instead: plateaus at 47.5%, below both RL runs.

Everything is open and reproducible: the capture proxy in OpenEnv, the trainer in TRL, the tasks, the SFT data, the training code and all 7 trained models. Bigger models and bigger runs next.

text:
The private equity takeover of local veterinary clinics is one of the most predatory scams happening in America right now.

Last month, our 3-year-old rescue dog threw up twice and seemed a little lethargic. Just acting off. We got nervous and rushed him to the local 24-hour emergency animal hospital.

Before a vet had even stepped into the room, the receptionist slid an iPad across the desk:

"Emergency exam intake fee is $385 non-refundable just for the doctor to evaluate him."

Fine. You pay it because you love your dog.

The vet walks in, checks his gums for twenty seconds, feels his stomach, and walks back out. Five minutes later, she returns with a printed estimate:

Full blood panel: $650.
Abdominal ultrasound: $900.
Overnight hospitalization with IV: $1,400.
Exploratory sedation: $800.
Total estimated cost: $3,750.

I asked the vet: "He ate a weird piece of grass earlier. Can we just start with an anti-nausea injection and monitor him for a couple of hours?"

The vet looked me dead in the eyes with a straight face and said:

"You can do that. But if he has a complete gastrointestinal blockage, he could go septic and pass away by sunrise."

Pure emotional manipulation.

They know your pet is family, so they hold your empathy hostage to hit corporate revenue quotas.

We declined the package, paid the exam fee, and took him home. Fed him white rice and boiled chicken. Two hours later, he drank a bowl of water, took a long nap, and was running circles around the yard by 8:00 AM the next morning.

Massive private corporations bought out almost every neighborhood mom-and-pop vet clinic, turned them into profit mills, and weaponized our love for animals into maximum billing.

Has modern veterinary medicine become an emotional shakedown, or are people just ungrateful for specialized care?

Let’s talk about my biggest onchain conviction play. $Crawl

@crawlnetwork is one of those projects where I think people are looking at the first product & missing the actual company being built.

The obvious thing is “crypto LLM.” The bigger thesis is a model that becomes the intelligence layer for an entire industry, with the industry itself economically incentivized to build its training data.

Think about what that means. Crypto already produces an absurd amount of information, but it is scattered across chains, contracts, docs, GitHub, governance, funding rounds, markets, research and social data. Today you pay different companies to organize pieces of it, then manually connect the pieces. Nansen can charge up to $1,800/month, Glassnode up to $999, Chainalysis sells six-figure contracts, and the broader alternative-data market is already measured in billions.

An industry-specific LLM changes the product entirely. Instead of another terminal that shows you data, you have a model that understands the relationships inside the data and can reason across them. A fund can ask about an ecosystem, an agent can investigate a protocol, a wallet can interpret onchain activity, a protocol can analyze its competitors, and an application can build its own intelligence layer on top of the model. The model becomes the interface to the industry’s information.

That is already a massive opportunity. But Crawlnet’s more interesting idea is how they are trying to build it.

They are turning the training corpus into an economy.

Crawlers are paid to find and produce the information the model needs. 60% of fees goes toward browsers and GPUs, 40% toward crawlers. Protocols can pay to get information into the corpus. The network takes that constantly expanding information, trains the model, and distributes the weights. The thing being produced by the network isn’t a token, a dashboard or a static database. It’s training data.

This is where the $axs  style gamification matters. Game showed that you can turn participation in a digital economy into an economically incentivized game. Crawlnet is applying a similar concept to data production: instead of people playing to produce game assets, operators crawl to produce information that becomes part of an AI’s brain. The network can potentially turn thousands of people and agents into a distributed data-collection workforce, with rewards tied to the economic value of what they contribute.

That creates a much more interesting flywheel than a normal LLM company has.

More crawlers create more data. More data creates a larger and potentially better crypto model. A better model attracts more applications, agents, protocols and funds. More usage creates more economic demand. More economic demand funds more crawling and compute. The network can therefore keep expanding the thing that makes the model valuable. And the starting point is already surprisingly large.

Three days in, Queen v2 is 75.5M parameters, trained from scratch on 88.9M tokens and 79,250 pages. 34,282 pages were collected by its own crawlers. The corpus already contains information on 29,000 projects, 13,162 funding rounds and 8,341 investors. Roughly 160 crawlers are active across 644 domains. The previous 42M-parameter model reportedly won a blind test 81–16.  It’s the distance between 75.5M and what the network could eventually train on.

quoted_text:
What Menlo has done over the last 24 months is exceptional.

Yes, they did Anthropic’s round at $4BN that will make them $50BN+ as a firm. NICE!

But they then took that and went f****** hard. They do Lovable, Higgsfield, Legora.

They compounded the brand win of Anthropic to cement their position from respectfully a slightly ageing firm to being a dominant venture leader at the forefront with Thrive, a16z, Benchmark etc.

It is incredible to see and I sat down with @venkyganesan to shoot the s*** on this.

1. Every Seed Investment Is an Option Bet

Seed-stage deals function as financial options to discover true outlier potential before committing major capital. VCs must construct a broad enough portfolio to secure sufficient at-bats, only sizing up their position when quantifiable, revenue-based metrics prove an outlier has emerged.

2. What Is the First Sign of the AI Wave Cracking?

Market cycles rarely collapse due to equity write-downs. They fracture when levered debt defaults occur. When market participants take on heavy leverage during an AI boom, precise timing becomes as critical as being directionally correct, making debt obligations the primary failure vector when cycles turn.

3. Why Every VC Must Now Prioritize IRR

Every startup in the current landscape writes a structural tax to the Mag 7 and hyperscalers for compute and foundation models. Because LPs can buy index exposure to those same public tech giants without fees or carry, private VCs must generate outsized IRR performance, beating public markets by at least 1,000 basis points, to justify private capital allocation.

4. Why LPs Wanting Smaller Funds and Slower Deployment Is BS

LPs cannot demand both smaller fund sizes and multi-year deployment paces in the middle of a generational platform shift. Because AI startups face immense capital requirements to scale compute, VC firms that refuse to deploy capital rapidly will watch competitors step in and capture the category winners.

5. The Theory of Reflexivity and How It's Causing Markups

Reflexivity creates self-reinforcing loops where fast revenue growth triggers rapid valuation markups, attracting elite human and financial capital that further accelerates growth. However, when copycat investors chase markups for momentum rather than underlying fundamentals, reflexive valuation bubbles inflate until market realities force an inevitable correction.

6. Sometimes You Pay Up Because You Have Unique Insight

Premium entry prices are not always the result of irrational bidding. They often stem from an investor's ability to recognize a fundamentally larger total addressable market than the consensus. When a VC possesses unique conviction around an expanding market opportunity, paying above current rates reflects calculated foresight rather than price-taking behavior.

7. There's No Limit to What a Person Can Do as Long as They Don't Care Who Gets the Credit

Personal ego remains one of the most expensive liabilities in venture capital and company building. True long-term success requires setting aside individual notoriety, focusing ruthlessly on generating LP returns, and empowering teammates and founders without worrying about who receives the public credit.
